item.title: Mamunur Rashid in critical condition, receiving treatment in ICU
item.description:
Actor and playwright Mamunur Rashid is receiving treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) of a hospital after developing pneumonia. He has been receiving treatment at a hospital in Dhaka for the past four days.

Physicians are trying to improve his condition, although his blood oxygen levels continue to fluctuate.

Director Animesh Aich confirmed Mamunur Rashid’s illness to Prothom Alo. He visited the actor at the hospital on Wednesday afternoon and spoke to him.

Animesh Aich told Prothom Alo, “I spoke to him. He was speaking normally. However, his oxygen saturation levels are fluctuating. The physicians are providing treatment with great care.”

Mamunur Rashid travelled to Khulna to attend a festival before being admitted to hospital. He fell ill the day after returning from the event. His family has since requested everyone not to crowd the hospital.

Mamunur Rashid has previously suffered a serious illness that required treatment in the ICU. On 30 April 2025, he fell ill aboard an aircraft while travelling to the United States.

Medical examinations at a hospital there revealed pneumonia in both lungs and a bloodstream infection. He recovered after spending six days in the ICU and returned home.

After staying in the United States for an extended period, Mamunur Rashid returned to Bangladesh on 14 January 2026. He subsequently resumed acting.

Mamunur Rashid has worked in theatre, television and films in Bangladesh for more than five decades. Alongside acting, he is also widely recognised as a playwright and theatre director.

He played an important role in advancing theatrical practice in the country after independence. In 1972, he founded Aranyak, one of the country's leading theatre groups.

Mamunur Rashid was born on 29 February 1948 in Bhabanadatta village in Ghatail, Tangail. He developed an interest in acting during his school years.

While studying at Dhaka Polytechnic Institute, he became more deeply involved in theatre. He later obtained bachelor's and master's degrees in political science from the University of Dhaka.

Mamunur Rashid began writing plays for television in the 1960s. His first television play was Chenamukh.

After independence, he established Aranyak Theatre Group. Some of the group's notable stage productions include Ora Kadam Ali, Iblish, Shingkranti, Rarang and Che'r Cycle.

Alongside his work in theatre and television, Mamunur Rashid has also gained recognition among audiences for his performances in films.

His notable films include Monpura, Mrittika Maya, Nekabborer Mahaproyan, Shankhachil, Bhuban Majhi, Pap Punno, Patalghar and Borbaad. He received the National Film Award for his performance in Monpura.

item.title: Egypt says 31 dead in Cairo fire after fuel truck overturns
item.description:
EGYPT-FIRE

A fire erupted in Egyptian capital Cairo on Wednesday killing at least 31 people, the health ministry said, after a fuel truck reportedly overturned on a packed highway.

AFP footage showed a huge fireball and thick black smoke rising above the densely populated capital’s Al-Waraq neighbourhood as motorists sounded their horns and scrambled to get away. Surrounding buildings appeared to escape the flames.

State media reported that the fire broke out when a truck loaded with fuel overturned on Cairo’s Ring Road—a crowded highway linking different parts of the capital—and burst into flames, engulfing nearby vehicles.

The health ministry said 39 ambulances were sent to the scene and 15 people were taken to hospital with injuries, four of them in critical condition.

“The scene was terrifying,” Abdel Rahman Khalil told AFP, saying he arrived shortly after the crash and saw the overturned fuel truck engulfed in flames.

AFP images showed a grisly aftermath with cars burned out, as firefighters doused the truck’s wreckage.

Egypt’s public prosecutor said an investigation had been opened and DNA tests were being carried out to identify badly burned victims.

The health ministry said it had raised its emergency alert level and Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar had travelled to the scene and nearby hospitals.

Charred wreckage

The health minister’s spokesman told state-linked al-Qahera News that “the Ring Road has been reopened, and the remnants of the accident have been cleared.”

Footage carried by Al-Qahera News showed the charred truck’s wreckage being removed, while traffic partially resumed around it.

A spokesperson for the Egyptian Cabinet told local media that Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly had ordered an investigation into the causes of the accident.

He said the government was awaiting a full clarification before determining “future measures regarding the transport of petroleum products and ensuring safety and security during such transport operations”.

Road deaths

Egypt, with its informal residential areas and often dilapidated infrastructure, has suffered several deadly fires in recent years.

Fire escapes, smoke detectors and alarms are rare and in many areas, warrens of narrow roads make it hard for fire engines to reach disaster sites.

Car crashes are also common, and often blamed on reckless driving, poor maintenance and uneven law enforcement, with traffic laws also being widely flouted.

Last year, nearly 6,000 people died in road accidents across the country, according to Egypt’s state statistics agency.

The year before, more than 5,200 road deaths were recorded across the country, according to authorities.

In August, at least 18 people, many of them teenagers, were killed in northern Egypt when two pick-up trucks carrying agricultural day-labourers crashed.

item.title: Jamaat seeks retraction of Australian newspaper report on Shafiqur Rahman, issues legal notice
item.description:
Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami has protested against a report published by Australian newspaper "The Australian" concerning the visit to Australia by its Ameer, Shafiqur Rahman, who is also the Leader of the Opposition in the Jatiya Sangsad.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the party’s Secretary-General and former member of parliament, Mia Golam Porwar, described the report as “false, misleading and defamatory”.

He demanded its immediate retraction and a public apology from the newspaper.

According to the Jamaat statement, on behalf of the Jamaat chief, Barrister Mir Ahmad Bin Quasem, Shafiqur Rahman’s foreign affairs adviser and an MP, has formally served a “concerns notice” to the newspaper’s publisher, Nationwide News Pty Limited.

The notice was issued under Section 12A of Australia’s Defamation Act 2005 (NSW), the statement said.

The statement further said Jamaat had identified seven statements and implications in the report as defamatory. The notice demands that the newspaper correct and retract the report, issue an apology and preserve all relevant documents. It also requires a written response within 48 hours.

"The Australian" reported that Shafiqur Rahman arrived in Sydney on Friday for a five-day visit. During his stay, Australian immigration adviser Raymond Solomon lodged an application calling for his visa to be cancelled.

In response, Jamaat said the report was published on the very day of the parliamentary-authorised official visit. The party described the publication as a calculated attempt to discredit the Opposition in the international arena.

Jamaat alleged that a key basis for the report was the application submitted by Solomon. It further claimed that the newspaper had concealed his identity as the writer and director of “Baba”, a film about Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and his family.

What the report said

“The Australian” reported that Shafiqur Rahman had praised Yahya Sinwar, the Hamas leader in Gaza, describing him as a “hero and martyr”. It also said that he had expressed grief over the death of another Hamas leader, Ismail Haniyeh, and prayed that he be accepted as a martyr.

Responding to these allegations, Mia Golam Porwar said that portraying support for the freedom and dignity of the Palestinian people as endorsement of terrorism amounted to a deliberate distortion.

He maintained that Shafiqur Rahman opposed attacks on civilians, irrespective of their nationality or religion.

“The Australian” newspaper also alleged that Shafiqur Rahman had described Jamaat leaders convicted of crimes against humanity in 1971 as “martyrs”.

In response, Jamaat said that the post in question had not been written by Shafiqur Rahman but had been published after his account was hacked. The party also said that evidence had been submitted to the law enforcement authorities and that one person had been arrested in connection with the incident.

Mia Golam Porwar also stated that the United Nations and international human rights organisations had raised questions about the fairness of the trials conducted by the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT).

“The Australian” reported that Shafiqur Rahman had not responded to requests for comment. 

However, Mia Golam Porwar said that neither he nor anyone else from the party had been contacted before the report was published.

He described this as a clear violation of the fundamental principles of journalism.

The report also noted that Jamaat had fielded no female candidates in Bangladesh’s 2026 parliamentary election.

It further stated that Raymond Solomon had raised questions in his application about Shafiqur Rahman’s relationship with Iran and his diplomatic position.

During his visit, Shafiqur Rahman attended a gathering of expatriate Bangladeshis in Campbelltown, Sydney, as well as a luncheon hosted by the Australian National Imams Council in Chullora, according to the report.

It may be noted that Shafiqur Rahman left Sydney on Tuesday (24 November) to return home following his four-day visit to Australia. He cancelled a scheduled visit to Malaysia, citing urgent necessity.

In his statement, Mia Golam Porwar said that press freedom did not constitute a licence to disseminate falsehoods.

He warned that the party would pursue all available legal remedies unless the newspaper retracted the report, published Shafiqur Rahman’s response and issued an apology.

item.title: India urges US to resolve tariff dispute in trade talks
item.description:
India has said that trade concerns should be addressed through ongoing talks with Washington, after the United States proposed raising tariffs on Indian goods to 17 per cent.

“India and the United States are engaged in negotiations for a Bilateral Trade Agreement,” New Delhi’s commerce ministry said late Wednesday, saying it was working towards an “early conclusion” of a deal.

“It has been India’s position that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of these negotiations,” the statement added.

The two countries reached an interim trade agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.

However, the US Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs days later, fuelling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.

The two sides have been negotiating ever since.

However, on Wednesday, Washington—after a months-long probe into alleged excess production—proposed a 17 per cent rate on India.

“India engaged constructively throughout this investigation,” New Delhi added.

“In response...the Department of Commerce stated that India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector.”

The new tariffs face a period of public comment before taking effect.

Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said in October that the talks had reached “a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult”.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on a visit to India shortly after, was more upbeat, saying the two sides were “about as close as you can be without having an executed agreement”.

item.title: Power has changed hands, but will the economy's old ailments be cured?
item.description:
A few weeks after the interim government took office, a committee led by Debapriya Bhattacharya submitted a nearly 400-page white paper. This document remains important for understanding the concept of ‘institutional theft’ during Sheikh Hasina’s tenure. It highlighted how around $16 billion was siphoned abroad annually, 23 to 40 per cent of development project expenditures were embezzled, and how the statistics of GDP, inflation, and poverty were manipulated to create an inflated growth narrative amid a debt burden of more than Tk 18 trillion. I call this manipulation ''Hasinomics''. Even though the white paper contains what happened, understanding how it happened is essential to preempt future .

The underlying structure of Hasinomics

Firstly, after the first decade of the current millennium, the economy was stalling due to limitations in infrastructure, skills, and the investment environment. Instead of focusing on improving skills or the investment environment, the ruling elite opted for a surge in infrastructure development. The issue wasn’t financial; it was political economy. A non-refundable offer was placed before the emerging oligarchs—support the government's political agenda and in return receive mega projects and business opportunities without any oversight. What was the outcome?

While there were some visible results, if the mega projects truly spread benefits across the economy, there would have been an impact on productivity calculations. But that didn’t happen. The country couldn’t move beyond exporting ready-made garments and manpower. Compared to the size of the economy, imports or foreign investments were significantly lower than almost all Southeast Asian countries. This raises the question, was there no chance for an active industrial policy? Or did the bargaining between oligarchs and rulers stall the policy?

Secondly, there are even more uncomfortable issues. Weak revenue, the financial risks of power purchase agreements, and the woes of the banking sector are generally viewed as separate problems. But seen alongside the informal money transfer system ‘hundi’, it’s clear that the massive informal sector was not an accident of Hasinomics; rather, it was part of its framework.

Starting with taxes, due to political bargaining, the ruling elite couldn’t impose taxes on the wealthy, nor could they impose higher taxes on the general public out of fear of political backlash. Thus, low tax revenues were a destined outcome. Meanwhile, a weakly overseen banking sector was essential for ‘crony arrangements’ with oligarchs.

Part of that money was transferred abroad through hundi, bypassing formal accounting. The flip side of this transaction was informal remittances, which kept consumer spending buoyant domestically. In this sense, structural transformation was impossible during Hasina’s era. Transformation meant the end of informality, and informality was the fabric of Hasinomics.

Without the July uprising, it’s hard to predict how disastrous the outcome of this model would have been. However, it’s possible to conjecture. The chronic current account deficit would eventually force an increase in domestic savings. Sooner or later, electricity bills would have to be paid, the banking crisis would deepen—there wouldn’t be a way out. With fiscal constraints pressing down, social security spending would decline. The potential for growth by increasing crony capital and informal labour would eventually run out, trapping Bangladesh in a lower-middle-income status, with even greater inequality. Unfortunately, even after the fall of the Hasina government, this outcome remains quite possible.

Where is the implementation plan

The interim government was aware of the problem. The economic white paper was a document looking back; meanwhile, a task force led by KAS Murshid submitted a nearly 550-page report to look forward. Instead of grand five-year plans, they emphasised quickly implementable steps, such as forming a regulatory reform commission, an oversight committee for the National Board of Revenue, revamping the BRTA, creating a new independently operated aviation entity instead of a loss-making airline, and allowing polytechnics to offer two-year technology bachelor's degrees.

But virtually none of these have seen the light of day. The reason is probably quite simple—the interim government did justice to its name concerning economic matters. They merely managed the emergency situation, leaving the burden of structural reforms for the elected government.

The elected BNP government has taken a long-term vision. During Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s time, the Planning Commission introduced the five-year strategic framework with the slogan ''From Fragility to Prosperity''. It is a ''living document'' reviewable annually, based on a three-phase strategy of recovery, re-establishment, and reconstruction.

The target is a trillion-dollar economy by 2034, and to increase foreign investment from 0. 45 per cent of GDP to 2. 5 per cent. Structured around five pillars—social security, education-health, energy and industrialisation, good governance, and social harmony—it also includes trade liberalisation, export diversification, and a stability fund.

All three documents acknowledge that the manipulations during Hasina’s era have left deep scars. However, are the questions raised earlier about industrial policy truly of the past? Or do the same questions await a democratic government?

The politics of weathering the crisis storm

During the tumultuous days of July, alongside political graffiti, images of the Japanese manga ‘One Piece’ were painted on Dhaka’s walls. Eventually, this symbol spread to the Gen-Z movements in Indonesia, Nepal, the Philippines, and Madagascar. The flag in the story was a symbol of freedom in the fight against authoritarian rule. But the intense anger that drove the youth to splash paint on the walls and spill their blood on the streets—the economic escape routes from its sources, such as slow growth, high inflation, and unsustainable debt burdens—are still not visible. The multifaceted crisis in banking, energy, inflation, revenue, and foreign transactions rooted in the ousted regime could at any time derail any long-term strategy.

Experiences from other countries also provide ample cause for caution. When movements were gathering momentum on Bangladesh campuses, almost simultaneously, Kenya’s Gen-Z protesters stormed their parliament against a finance bill proposing tax hikes and service cuts. The bill was brought by a government that came to power promising reforms after the financial devastation left by their corrupt predecessors. Reforms are difficult; and that difficulty tempts the government to avoid tough decisions and even revert to old habits.

But that path isn’t safe either. In 1990, economists Rudiger Dornbusch and Sebastian Edwards showed that focusing on growth and distribution while ignoring stability and external constraints ultimately leads to crisis in macroeconomic populism. On the other hand, research by the Nobel-winning Turkish-American economist Daron Acemoglu and colleagues suggests that democratisation boosts per capita income by about one-fifth in the long run. Another Turkish-American economist Dani Rodrik’s 1999 research shows that countries that manage social conflict well are also remarkable at handling external shocks.

Whether bank reform, energy, or revenue constraints, the government must soon make tough decisions, where both the ailing domestic economy alongside external world risks are increasing. A democracy that doesn’t just end with elections but heals social and political wounds can open the path to prudent macroeconomic policy. Perhaps that is the economic condition for holding true to the promises of July’s blood.

# Jyoti Rahman is the Chairperson of the Panam Institute and an Applied Macroeconomist

item.title: Jubo Dal's Nayan says tip-off led him to 20 suspected Awami League members
item.description:
Jubo Dal leader Rabiul Islam Nayan, along with party activists, surrounded a house in Dhaka's Gulshan on Wednesday afternoon, climbed over its boundary wall, searched the rooms and brought out 20 people on suspicion that they were Awami League leaders and activists, before handing them over to the police.
Gulshan police confirmed the detentions, according to Prothom Alo. Nayan is member secretary of the Dhaka Metropolitan South unit of Jubo Dal, and the incident took place at house No 74 on Road 41.
The incident took place at house No 74 on Road 41 in Gulshan. Nayan is member secretary of the Dhaka Metropolitan South unit of Jubo Dal. He detained 20 people from the house on suspicion that they were Awami League leaders and activists, then handed them to the police.
Nayan shared a video of the detention on his verified Facebook account. It shows signboards for a dental clinic and a salon on the ground floor of the building. He went there in the afternoon with party activists, posted them around the house and instructed them not to let anyone escape. He then climbed the boundary wall, entered the house, searched the rooms and brought people out.
Police personnel later brought several people downstairs one by one and gathered them in the building's parking area. In the video, a Jubo Dal activist is heard saying: "They came to carry out sabotage. We have caught all the Chhatra League and Jubo League people." Nayan was also seen searching various rooms. At one point, he handed the passports, mobile phones and wallets of several people to the police. He was heard telling them: "Release those who are innocent."
After leaving the house, Nayan explained the incident to journalists. He said he had received information in the morning that several people from Gopalganj, the president of the Rangpur district Awami League, and some people led by the president of the Banani Thana Sramik League would hold a secret meeting at the house around 4pm. After receiving the information, they went there.
He also claimed that a section of a window at the back of the building had been cut to create an escape route. According to Nayan, several people fled through it after learning of their presence. He said police had detained 20 to 22 people in all.
Nayan said they were making plans there with December approaching. He added that they would resist Awami League leaders and activists if they planned sabotage anywhere in the Dhaka metropolitan area.
The video also shows Nayan and his followers chanting in front of the house. They are heard saying: "Hasina, come back to the country; let us see who saves you" and "Catch the League, put them in jail." Police later took the detained people away in vehicles.
Prothom Alo reported that Gulshan police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Abu Zayed Mohammad Najmun Nur confirmed that 20 people had been detained from a house in Gulshan on suspicion of being leaders and activists of the Awami League, whose activities are banned.
According to the OC, Jubo Dal leaders and activists had detained them and informed the police, who then went to the house and brought them to the police station. Police are checking whether any cases have been filed against the detained individuals.
Another video on Nayan's Facebook account shows him detaining Rahmatullah Shanto, who identified himself as a Jubo League leader, and handing him to the police. Before handing him over, Nayan is seen giving him cheese and persimmons to eat.
On Tuesday night, Nayan also detained Javed Didar, a leader of the banned Awami League, from the Paltan area of the capital and handed him to the police. He shared a video of that incident on Facebook as well. It shows Nayan giving the detained man boiled eggs, water and coffee after his detention.

item.title: Fire at MP Nusrat Tabassum’s home: Probe finds no evidence of petrol bomb attack
item.description:
A high-level investigation committee formed by the Home Ministry has found no evidence of sabotage or a petrol bomb attack in the fire at the house of reserved-seat MP and National Citizen Party (NCP) leader Nusrat Tabassum in Kushtia. However, it has recommended further investigation to establish the exact cause of the blaze.
The 4-member committee submitted its 15- to 20-page sealed report to the ministry in Dhaka on Wednesday morning, following a one-time extension of its deadline.
Committee head Ahmed Mahbub-ul-Islam, deputy director of the Kushtia Local Government Division, confirmed the submission.
He said the committee members finalized the report at a meeting before sending it to Dhaka in a sealed envelope. However, he declined to comment on its contents, citing confidentiality.
The other members of the committee are Major Asrarul Haque, additional director (operations) of the Border Guard Bangladesh's Kushtia Sector; Delwar Hossain, additional superintendent of Kushtia Police (Bheramara Circle); and Wadud Hossain, assistant director of Kushtia Fire Service and Civil Defence.
Several sources involved in the investigation said the committee could not specifically determine the cause or point of origin of the fire and, therefore, recommended further investigation.
The report identified 4 to 5 possible causes of the fire, including a cigarette ember inside the house and a possible short circuit involving old electrical wiring.
A committee member, requesting anonymity, said the report analyzed the possible causes and recommended further investigation into each of them.
Asked whether the fire was an act of sabotage or a petrol bomb attack, the member said the report described the possibility of a petrol bomb causing the fire as very low.
During the investigation, committee members recorded detailed statements from residents of the house and several eyewitnesses from the surrounding area. They identified the possible causes by analyzing the accounts and the circumstances surrounding the incident, the sources said.
The Home Ministry formed the 4-member committee on November 12, considering the significance of the fire at the MP's grandmother's house.
Initially, the committee was asked to submit its report within 3 working days. The deadline was later extended by another 7 working days from November 16, with the extended period ending on Tuesday.
The fire broke out late on the night of November 11 at the house in Bagoan village of Daulatpur upazila in Kushtia.
The following day, Nusrat Tabassum filed a case with Daulatpur Police Station, naming 8 local leaders of the banned Chhatra League, Jubo League and Swechchhasebak League and accusing another 25 to 30 unidentified people.

item.title: 16 crude bombs recovered from CNG in Keraniganj; 2 AL activists held
item.description:
Police recovered 16 crude bombs from a CNG-run auto-rickshaw at a checkpoint in the Naya Bazar area of Keraniganj on Wednesday afternoon and arrested two Awami League activists, whose activities are banned, in this connection.
The arrestees were identified as Nazim and Akash, both reported to be local AL activists of the Dhaka-2 Constitutional area. Police arrested them on the spot for carrying the explosives.
Officer-in-Charge Ruhul Kuddus of Keraniganj Model Police Station said a police team intercepted a CNG auto-rickshaw at a regular checkpoint in Naya Bazar and seized 16 crude bombs (cocktails) from the vehicle.
Later, a bomb disposal unit of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) arrived at the scene and safely detonated the recovered crude bombs.
A case was filed under the Explosive Substances Act with Keraniganj Model Police Station on Wednesday evening, the OC added.

item.title: JU students block highway over fellow’s alleged assault by Army men
item.description:
Jahangirnagar University (JU) students blocked the Dhaka-Aricha highway for around two and a half hours on Wednesday evening, protesting the alleged assault of a fellow student by some Army personnel.
The protesters took to the highway near the university's Dairy Gate around 7:30pm and blocked it, disrupting traffic and causing long tailbacks on both sides.
They placed four demands, including the dismissal and prosecution of the accused, a public apology from them in person, accountability for repeated incidents of this nature and payment of the victim's medical expenses.
The protesters, however, withdrew the blockade around 10:00pm after the senior Army officials talked to Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Md Nurul Islam and assured him they would look into the matter, said the VC.
The victim, Aurangzeb Ramjan, is a student of the Department of Economics from the 2023-24 academic session and a resident of Mir Mosharraf Hossain Hall.
Ramjan alleged that some Army men stopped the auto-rickshaw he was travelling in while on his way to provide tuition through Bismail in the afternoon and hit him with a stick.
Photo: UNB
“When I protested, the personnel took me to a nearby room and kicked and beat me,” he said.
JU Pro-VC (Academic) Prof Dr Md Shamsul Alam said the university administration was sympathetic to the students' protest and was working to resolve the issue.
Photo: UNB
Pro-VC (Administration) Prof Dr Mohammad Nazrul Islam said the VC had contacted the relevant higher authorities and a team was expected to visit the university to meet the victim and witnesses.

item.title: Illumina Innovation Day held in Dhaka
item.description:
Illumina, a global DNA sequencing leader, and its Bangladesh partner Invent Technologies Ltd organized “Illumina Innovation Day – Bangladesh 2026” at Renaissance Dhaka Gulshan Hotel on Tuesday, bringing together clinicians, scientists, and laboratory leaders to explore genomics applications in cancer care and infectious disease surveillance.
Participants included representatives from icddr,b, Child Health Research Foundation, Bangladesh Medical University, BIRDEM, Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission, and leading hospitals and diagnostic centres.
Illumina experts Fang Min Tan and Bi Chonglei showcased the MiSeq i100 benchtop sequencer, highlighting its applications in cancer research, genomic profiling, and data analysis, said a press release.
Invent Technologies General Manager (Life Science) Sheikh Md Selim Al Din discussed how genomic sequencing can help identify pathogens, monitor dengue, influenza, and tuberculosis outbreaks, and detect antimicrobial resistance within 24-48 hours.
Dr Mustak Ibn Ayub presented precision medicine in cancer management in Bangladesh and moderated a panel discussion on clinical genomics, testing costs, turnaround times, and developing local expertise.
Speakers stressed that expanding domestic genomic testing capacity could reduce costs and waiting times while strengthening cancer care and public health surveillance.
Invent Technologies also announced that its Central Dogma Lab in Mirpur, equipped with a MiSeq i100 Plus, is open for researchers and clinicians to test their own samples.

item.title: Mulder runs riot as Bangladesh suffer innings defeat
item.description:
Bangladesh endured another disappointing batting collapse as Wiaan Mulder’s career-best seven-wicket haul powered South Africa to an emphatic innings and 219-run victory in the second and final Test at SuperSport Park in Centurion on Wednesday, completing a 2-0 series sweep.
Mulder, who had earlier struck a century in South Africa’s only innings, returned figures of 7-31 to bundle Bangladesh out for 184 in their second innings, handing the hosts victory inside three days and further strengthening their position at the top of the World Test Championship standings.
The defeat exposed Bangladesh’s continued struggles against quality pace bowling, particularly in challenging South African conditions, as they followed up their first-innings collapse for just 91 with another batting failure.
Resuming the third day with a commanding 403-run lead, South Africa declared their first innings at 494-7 without adding to their overnight total, leaving Bangladesh with a daunting task to stay in the contest.
Bangladesh made a relatively encouraging start, with openers Tanzid Hasan Tamim and Mahfijul Islam Rony putting together 58 runs, their first half-century opening partnership of the series and a record stand for Bangladesh against South Africa.
However, the resistance did not last long as Mulder struck twice in consecutive overs to remove Tanzid, who edged behind for 29, and Mominul Haque, who departed for a five-ball duck.
Mahfijul, who had shown some promise in the first innings as well, again failed to convert his start into a substantial contribution, falling leg-before to Marco Jansen for 38.
At 78-3, Bangladesh were in danger of another early collapse, but Towhid Hridoy counterattacked with an aggressive 41, offering some resistance against the South African attack. He eventually fell to Kagiso Rabada, caught at gully by Zubayr Hamza.
Captain Najmul Hossain Shanto managed 12, while Hridoy's effort remained the brightest feature of another difficult batting display.
Mulder then took complete control, claiming five wickets in the space of just 17 deliveries as Bangladesh's lower order offered little resistance. Jansen wrapped up the innings by dismissing Khaled Ahmed, with Mulder completing the catch at third man.
Reflecting on Bangladesh's performance, Shanto acknowledged that his side had failed to adapt to the conditions and execute their plans.
“We know that conditions are tough. Our batters couldn't adapt, especially in the first innings. We had to come in with a good plan but our execution was off,” Shanto said after the match.
He identified catching, top-order batting and execution as key areas requiring improvement, while pointing to Hridoy's innings as one of the few positives.
For South Africa, the victory was another demonstration of their bowling depth, with Mulder's all-round contribution earning him Player of the Match honours. His century and seven-wicket haul made him the first South African to score a hundred and take seven wickets in the same Test.
“Really special, never thought I'd achieve that,” Mulder said. “I play different roles in this team. It doesn't matter what question is asked of me, it's about contributing and helping win.”
South Africa captain Aiden Markram credited his team's collective effort, while acknowledging Bangladesh's competitiveness in the opening Test at the Wanderers.
“We expected a tussle, we got lucky with the toss, and then our bowlers did the work well,” Markram said.
The series sweep keeps South Africa firmly on course for a place in the 2027 World Test Championship final. They will next host England in a three-Test series beginning in Johannesburg on December 17.
For Bangladesh, the 2-0 defeat leaves plenty to address, particularly their inability to cope with pace and bounce away from home. Their brief moments of resistance in Centurion were not enough to prevent another comprehensive defeat.

item.title: Jamaat to stage nationwide protests Thursday against Awami League violence
item.description:
Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami will hold rallies across all districts on Thursday as part of its program to protest what it describes as nationwide violence and arson by the ousted Awami League and to press for the seven-point demand of the 11-party alliance.
Jamaat Secretary General Mia Golam Porwar in a statement on Wednesday urged all to make the program a success.
Porwar said the party would also protest what it described as the government's failure to maintain law and order amid the evil attempts by the ousted Awami League, which faces a ban on its activities.
He called on the people in the respective districts to join the program spontaneously and sought cooperation from all citizens to make them a success.
As part of its announced program, the party staged demonstrations across all divisional cities, except Dhaka, on Wednesday.

item.title: Daniel Hahn on the translator's craft
item.description:
Daniel Hahn is a British writer, editor, and award-winning literary translator working across Portuguese, Spanish, and French.
His British-English version includes José Eduardo Agualusa's A General Theory of Oblivion , shortlisted for the Man Booker International Prize. He has won the Independent Foreign Fiction Prize and the 2023 Ottaway Award.
In this conversation, he speaks with Shazed Ul Hoq Abir, an award-winning Bengali writer and translator, about translation as a craft, from capturing an author's effect to knowing when to stop.
Shazed Ul Hoq Abir: I recently translated Milan Kundera's The Unbearable Lightness of Being into Bengali. Kundera was upset when an English translator broke a character's near-endless inner monologue in The Joke into shorter sentences, because it altered the rhythm and stylistic intention of the original. Do you consider preserving an author's syntactical peculiarities, even when they sound unconventional in the target language, part of the translator's ethical responsibility?
Daniel Hahn: You used the word "intention" at one point in your question, and I think that is part of it. I'm always trying to think about what the effect of a piece of writing is because I want to preserve the effect. But sometimes that means changing other things, and sometimes the way I want to preserve something is by taking one long sentence and making it into two short sentences. It isn't necessarily the case that the best way of preserving the effect and the function of a 63-sentence story is keeping precisely 63 sentences.
There are often other considerations, and the syntax in every language is different in structure. There are lots of things that I would feel happy to change, so long as the change is in the service of keeping what I think is important about the story.
Do you believe that the translator should sometimes deliberately produce awkward English to preserve the aesthetic experience of the original?
I wouldn't choose 'awkward,' but I would often choose something where the experience of the reader, including what something sounds like and the effect of the sound, the sonority, might be privileged over something else. I don't think it's necessarily a matter of awkwardness, but rather something like this: if something sounds jagged and harsh in the original, I would like it to sound jagged and harsh in English. And if something sounds smooth and mellifluous in the original, I would like it to sound smooth and mellifluous in English. That means resisting the temptation to make everything smooth and mellifluous, which is an easy temptation. It isn't about what is 'awkward' or 'natural' in one language or another. It's about what the writer is doing to the reader, and I want to do the same thing to my reader.
How do you handle a novel that contains several dialects? How do you reproduce those varieties of the source language?
I have this problem quite a lot because I translate from three languages, all of which are big, multicontinental, colonial languages. The most extreme version I can think of is a novel I translated by a Mexican writer. The book was called I Don't Expect Anyone to Believe Me . The writer is Juan Pablo Villalobos, and he plays around with lots of different varieties of Spanish. He has characters from lots of different parts of the Spanish-speaking world, and they speak to each other using these different varieties of Spanish. So, they tease each other and refer to the fact that they speak these different varieties.
What I did not do was replace them with lots of different existing varieties of English. So, for example, I didn't make one of them speak Australian English or another Californian English or whatever. What I did was think about what the purpose of the differences was supposed to be. So, if there are two characters and one of them looks down on the other because they think that their variety of Spanish is the superior one, then there are ways of using English to show a kind of patronizing attitude in one character towards another.
You translate three or four novels a year, and your first drafts, at up to 4,000 to 5,000 words a day, are very quick, perhaps even "bad." Turning to your working method, what do you deliberately leave unresolved in such a draft?
Oh, yes, definitely; they are very bad.
So many things are left unresolved because I don't let anything slow me down.
If there is a word whose meaning or resonances I don't know, I will leave it in the source language. Again, if something complex is happening, like a bit of wordplay or an ambiguity, I will leave it untranslated or mark it for myself.
The aim is to keep going. Anything that slows me down gets a note, brackets, or an asterisk.
Sometimes I leave the word in the source language or write it in uppercase. So anything I actually translate is the stuff that can happen almost automatically. The first draft happens without very much thinking, and then I go back and fill in the gaps, which is to say, solve all the problems. Then I have to edit it 10,000 times. Well, 8,000, not 10,000. I'm exaggerating.
Do you normally read an entire book before beginning its translation, or do you prefer to discover the narrative as you translate it?
I prefer to discover it as I go along. I know a lot of translators feel anxious about that. It does sometimes happen that I've already read a book for some other purpose. But my favourite way is to go straight in and make that first draft the point of discovery, replicating my own reading experience in the hope that another reader will have it too.
How do you know when a translation is finished? Does the text ever reach its fullest possible expression in the target language?
There is sometimes a point at which I think I've got it as far as I can. That doesn't make it perfect, but it's the limit of what I can do in that moment. Truthfully, and this will sound flippant, it's partly a deadline that decides when it's finished: I have a contract with a publisher, and they need it on Thursday. I delivered a book this morning, about 10 days after its deadline, and I could have gone on playing with it forever, but at some point it has to be published.
I also really like working with publishers, and I like being edited. So I think of what I 'finish' as just one stage that is done. What I deliver to a publisher is still malleable, still able to move around. So I don't have to think, 'What if it's not perfect?' Of course it's not perfect. It's reached a point where I am pleased with it, and I probably couldn't do much more without someone else's eyes on it.
The editor will look at it and send it back to me, followed by the copy editor. There's a big collaborative editorial process still to come. The genuine answer is that often it's not about finishing; it's just about stopping.
In one of your interviews, you mentioned that you usually share your translated drafts with the original authors. You welcome their comments and suggestions but ultimately retain the final say over the translation. I'm interested in the reasoning behind this position.
If you translate into English, it's not unusual, when working with a lot of different languages, to have an author who has a certain amount of English. Most of my authors would not be able to read their Czech translations or, indeed, their Tamil translations, their Polish translations, or whatever, but nearly all of them can read English, so their feedback and insights are valuable.
This does not mean that they use English the way I use English. And often, the authors I enjoy working with the most–not always, but often - are the ones who both have very good English and have a very good understanding of what my job is, which is not the same as their job.
That means, first of all, knowing how to be helpful without being control freaks. But it also means having some understanding of why I will be making the kinds of changes I'm making, so they don't say, 'I noticed that you reversed the order of these two clauses,' because they understand that this is the kind of thing that is sometimes part of my job.
It's also important to me that an author who is able to read English, which, as I say, is almost everyone I've translated, is happy with the way in which they have been represented. There's going to be a book with their name on the cover in which I have chosen all 60,000 words for them, and I understand why they would feel the need for some reassurance before that book goes out to be read by civilians.
Do you think relay translation is inherently problematic?
I think it can be. I don't think it has to be. I mean, it's always problematic in the sense that it's always going to create distortions, or, you know, you're going to be representing something different from what you're perhaps claiming to represent.
I don't think it's necessarily problematic in a political sense, though it can be that as well. But I do think there are ways of trying to do it as well as you can, as effortfully as you can, and as respectfully as you can. And then there are ways of doing what happened to Lin, which involve none of those things.
Recognition and visibility are often considered important motivations for people working in the arts. After honours like the International Dublin Literary Award and a Man Booker International shortlist, what keeps you motivated?
I think translation is an odd endeavour in lots of ways. But one of the things that characterises is wanting not only to show off one's own ego but also to amplify the work of other people. Because if I translate a novel, well, the person who will be most shown off is someone who is not me.
So, I think there is a slight difference, especially with a prize for a translation. There is a difference between that and many other kinds of acknowledgement. If I'm translating a novel because I want you to be able to read it, because you don't speak Portuguese, then any kind of mechanism that improves the chances of that novel finding readers is part of the same thing.
When a translation of mine is shortlisted for a prize or wins a prize, it's nice for the ego. But, more importantly, it is a way of amplifying the thing I'm trying to translate, which is the reason I'm translating it in the first place.
But on the whole, I suppose these things are about two things. They're about drawing attention to something that I've translated for the very purpose of drawing attention to. So that's important. And the other thing is making translation and translators visible, which I think is important in broader terms.
In the last 20 years, in a country like the UK, translators have become much more visible. And so, anything that helps with that also lifts, as the saying goes, 'a rising tide lifts all ships.' It doesn't just help the person who wins. It helps the visibility of the profession and the way the profession and the craft are valued.
Shazed Ul Hoq Abir is an award-winning Bengali writer and translator.

item.title: French opera, Bangla Jatrapala blend at French Week opening in Dhaka
item.description:
French opera singers Veronique Pain and pianist Fabrice Maitre brought together European operatic traditions and Bangla theatrical elements at a cultural concert marking the opening of French Week in Dhaka on Saturday evening.
Held at the Grand Ballroom of Hotel InterContinental Dhaka on November 21, the performance featured selections from French, American and Italian operas and musicals, incorporating the musical and theatrical sensibilities of traditional Bangla Jatrapala.
The nine-day event, titled “Semaine Francaise” (French Week), will run from November 21 to 29, commemorating the 50th death anniversary of French writer and former culture minister Andre Malraux, who supported Bangladesh's Liberation War in 1971.
The concert also marked the conclusion of a 10-day cultural festival celebrating the first anniversary of The Artist Club Limited.
The program was jointly organized by The Artist Club Limited and the Dhaka University Cultural Foundation (DUCF), under the patronage of the Ministry of Cultural Affairs and with support from the Embassy of France in Dhaka.
Before the concert, French Ambassador to Bangladesh Jean-Marc Sere-Charlet visited artist Rashed Khan's exhibition, “Nodir Golpo”, at the hotel. The exhibition, which was accompanied by Rashed Khan, chief coordinator Prof Dr AHM Mostafizur Rahman, and the French performers, formally concluded later that evening.
The opening ceremony began with welcome remarks from The Artist Club Limited Secretary General Maruf Kabir. Club President and musician Sujit Mustafa then highlighted the organization's activities, while Prof Dr AHM Mostafizur Rahman discussed the festival's objectives and the artistic connection between French and Bangla operatic traditions.
Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury welcomed the cultural collaboration between the two countries. State Minister for Cultural Affairs Ali Newaz Mahmud Khayyam and French Ambassador Jean-Marc Sere-Charlet also spoke about the importance of strengthening bilateral cultural relations.
The musical showcase featured excerpts from several celebrated productions, including “Carmen”, “La Belle Hélène”, “Porgy and Bess”, “Candide”, “My Fair Lady”, “Tosca” and “La Traviata”.
Pain led most of the vocal performances, while Maitre accompanied her on piano and presented solo instrumental passages and vocal performances of his own.
To help the audience follow the French-language selections, the performers provided brief English introductions explaining the stories, characters, and background of the pieces before each performance.
In a memorable moment towards the end of the evening, Pain and Maitre performed Bangladesh's national anthem, “Amar Sonar Bangla, Ami Tomay Bhalobashi”. The audience stood and joined in, bringing the cultural evening to a close.

item.title: GTA 6 generates $3.8bn in first-day sales, sets entertainment launch record
item.description:
Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) has generated an estimated $3.8 billion in retail sales on its first full day of release, setting a new record for the biggest entertainment launch across any medium.
Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of developer Rockstar Games, announced the figures on Friday, saying the estimates were based on sales recorded through the end of Thursday. The game had also secured 32.5 million pre-orders ahead of its release.
The opening-day revenue far exceeds the performance of other major entertainment releases. Spider-Man: Brand New Day, the highest-grossing film of the year so far, earned around $2.5 billion throughout its entire theatrical run.
The launch also triggered unprecedented online activity as millions of players rushed to download the game. Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare reported that PlayStation 5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times their usual levels around the launch.
New Zealand, the first country where the game became available, recorded a 14.8-fold increase in activity approximately four hours before the UK peak, indicating that some players may have changed their account regions to gain early access.
Cloudflare also reported significant increases in traffic to Rockstar's online services, with activity reaching 11.2 times normal levels in Australia and 9.3 times on the US East Coast. In Europe, the UK recorded the highest surge, at seven times its usual level, compared with 5.3 times in France and Germany.
GTA 6 has also surpassed the launch record of its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto V, which generated $1.15 billion in its first five days in 2013. The latest instalment continues Rockstar's nearly three-decade-old crime simulation franchise, known for its satirical portrayal of American society.
Set in Leonida, a fictional state inspired by Florida, the game follows two protagonists, Lucia and her partner Jason, as they navigate the criminal underworld.
The game's development is estimated to have cost more than $1 billion, potentially making it the most expensive video game ever produced.
Market research firm Sensor Tower expects the title to significantly affect the wider gaming industry, predicting that its popularity could reduce the time players spend on other single-player games by 10%. Its estimates suggest that approximately 75% of GTA 6 sales have come from PlayStation 5 users, with the remainder from Xbox players.
Meanwhile, gaming research firm Niko Partners projects that the game could generate more than $3 billion in worldwide sales this year.
Despite its extraordinary opening, GTA 6 could continue generating substantial revenue in the years ahead. Rockstar has yet to announce a PC release date or details about the game's multiplayer expansion, which is expected to allow players to connect online, complete missions, and interact with one another.
The multiplayer component could become another major source of income, following the success of GTA Online, which extended the commercial life of GTA 5 through in-game purchases of vehicles, properties, and other digital items.
The release has received widespread attention from gaming critics, with entertainment publication IGN describing it as an “uncompromisingly engineered” masterpiece.
The launch also placed considerable pressure on internet infrastructure. Virgin Media O2 reported breaking its evening traffic record as players downloaded the game's massive 212GB installation file.
However, the release has faced restrictions in some markets. Its graphic content has led to censorship in Japan, while the game has not been approved for sale in mainland China. In the United States, police departments also issued reminders that activities depicted in the game, including street racing, vehicle theft, and gun violence, remain criminal offences in real life.

item.title: Bangladesh’s first National Street Photo Festival highlights emerging talent
item.description:
Bangladesh’s emerging photographers have found a national platform to showcase their work as the country’s first National Street Photo Festival opened at La Galerie of Alliance Française de Dhaka (AFD) on Friday.
The festival brings together young photography enthusiasts from universities and colleges across the country, offering an opportunity to display their work, exchange creative ideas and build connections within the photography community.
The inaugural edition received an overwhelming response, attracting 2,721 photographs from around 700 student photographers representing 52 educational institutions. A three-member jury selected 44 photographs for the physical exhibition, while another 50 works are being showcased through digital screening.
Abir Abdullah, founder of the Alliance of Photographers and festival director, said the initiative was designed to recognize emerging talent and give young photographers an opportunity to share their perspectives through visual storytelling.
He said the response demonstrated the growing enthusiasm for photography among students and expressed hope that the festival would become a regular platform for nurturing young talent and strengthening the country's photography community.
This year's event also marks 200 years of photography, with a special tribute to renowned French photographer Henri Cartier-Bresson, whose work has had a lasting influence on street photography.
The opening ceremony was attended by Frédéric Inza, Deputy Head of Mission at the Embassy of France in Bangladesh; eminent photographer Shankar Shawjal; and photographer Saud Al Faisal, who served on the festival's jury.
Addressing the gathering, Inza praised the initiative and highlighted how photography, particularly street photography, makes art accessible to a wider audience. He observed that photographers can turn everyday scenes into meaningful visual narratives through their artistic vision and ability to capture fleeting moments.
He also commended the participation of approximately 700 students from 52 institutions and congratulated the organizers and young photographers.
The opening ceremony featured the announcement of the festival's top three winners, alongside 10 Honorable Mentions, recognizing outstanding creativity, originality and visual storytelling.
A central feature of the festival is its homage to Cartier-Bresson, celebrated for his concept of the 'decisive moment' — capturing a meaningful scene at precisely the right instant. The tribute connects the legacy of French photography with contemporary visual expression, encouraging young Bangladeshi photographers to discover and document the stories unfolding around them.

item.title: Nazifa Tushi wins Best Actress at Asian World Film Festival
item.description:
Bangladeshi actress Nazifa Tushi has won the Best Actress award at the 12th Asian World Film Festival (AWFF) in Los Angeles for her performance in “Roid”, marking another international achievement for the actress.
Tushi received the festival’s Snow Leopard award for her portrayal in the film, directed by Mejbaur Rahman Sumon. The recognition adds to her growing list of achievements and brings further international attention to Bangladeshi cinema.
The actress announced the news on social media on Friday, expressing her excitement and gratitude over the honor.
In her post, Tushi said she had already been overwhelmed with joy when “Roid” was selected to represent Bangladesh at the festival. She described the opportunity to present the country's cinema on an international platform, connecting Asian filmmakers with Hollywood and global audiences as a source of immense pride.
She also thanked the Almighty, her family and fans for their continued love, prayers and support. Tushi dedicated the award to the entire “Roid” team, acknowledging the contributions of its cast, crew and everyone involved in making the film.
The Snow Leopard Award is the festival's highest honor. Held annually in Los Angeles, the Asian World Film Festival showcases films from across Asia and helps bring regional cinema to international audiences.
Tushi's latest achievement marks another encouraging moment for Bangladesh's film industry, as local productions and performers continue to gain recognition beyond the country's borders.

item.title: Who will be Robert Pattinson’s ‘Bond girl’?
item.description:
The announcement of Robert Pattinson as the new 007 has sparked fresh excitement around the next chapter of the James Bond franchise. But while attention has focused on the actor taking over the iconic role, another question is beginning to dominate conversations: who will play the woman alongside him?
Several actresses have emerged as possible contenders, although no official casting announcements have been made.
Names circulating in industry discussions include Zendaya, Sydney Sweeney, Florence Pugh, Anya Taylor-Joy, Jodie Comer, Gemma Chan, Saoirse Ronan, Margaret Qualley and Simone Ashley.
Comer, known for her performances in Killing Eve and The Bikeriders , could bring a compelling combination of intensity and versatility to the franchise. Her experience portraying complex, independent characters makes her an interesting possibility for a Bond film looking to move beyond familiar romantic stereotypes.
Other names attracting attention include Zendaya, whose growing film career has made her one of Hollywood’s most prominent young stars, and Florence Pugh, who has established herself through a range of critically acclaimed performances. Sydney Sweeney, Anya Taylor-Joy and Gemma Chan have also been mentioned among potential candidates.
However, the role of the leading woman in a Bond film has changed considerably over the decades. Traditionally described as the “Bond girl”, female characters were often defined by their romantic involvement with the secret agent, with their appearances and relationships sometimes taking precedence over their individual stories.
Recent instalments have made efforts to challenge that formula. Women in the franchise have increasingly been portrayed as capable intelligence officers, formidable adversaries and independent characters with motivations of their own. The shift has also opened up conversations about greater diversity and more nuanced representations of gender and sexuality.
The next film could take that evolution further, giving its female characters stronger narrative roles rather than positioning them simply as romantic interests. Whether the franchise introduces a new ally, a rival agent or a complex antagonist, the casting choice could help shape the direction of Pattinson’s Bond era.
For now, the names remain speculative, and the producers have yet to reveal who will join the new 007 on screen. Until an official announcement arrives, the search for the next leading woman in the Bond universe remains one of the franchise’s biggest talking points.

item.title: Awami League man dies while making crude bombs
item.description:
An activist of the activities-banned Awami League was killed and at least four others injured in an explosion while allegedly making crude bombs in Shibganj Upazila of Chapainawabganj on Wednesday afternoon.
The incident occurred around 2:30pm in the Chouka area of Monakasha Union, beside a field under a banana tree.
The deceased was identified as Md Thomas Uddin, 35, son of Md Mortuza of Lombartola village in Bishwanathpur. His Facebook profile identified him as a member of Shibganj Upazila Krishak League and an Awami League activist.
Shibganj Police Station Officer-in-Charge Matiur Rahman said several people were making crude bombs at an isolated spot when one exploded, killing Thomas and injuring three to four others. The injured fled the scene afterwards.
Police recovered the body and sent it to the morgue of the 250-bed Chapainawabganj District Hospital for autopsy. An investigation is underway to determine the circumstances of the blast and identify those involved, the OC said.
Police Superintendent Gautam Kumar Biswas visited the scene later in the afternoon and said officers had recovered bomb-making materials along with the body.
Police had learned that the deceased was an activist of the activities-banned Awami League, although his organisational affiliation was still being verified, he said.
The SP said two or three other people might have been involved in making the explosives. Police suspect the materials were not being prepared for any legitimate purpose and are investigating the motive behind the activity.

Treating patients to healing rivers: A physician's mission to awaken public conscience
item.description:
Below the Doratana Bridge in Jashore (formerly Jessore), the river is covered with a green blanket of water hyacinth. In between, the little water that is visible is black.

For the people of the town, this sight has become quite normal. However, during a short holiday in Jashore, Sheikh Sadia Manowara Usha was aghast at this sight. It seemed like something needed to be done. On 5 November, she took to Facebook, asking for suggestions on initiating a cleanup of the Bhairab River covered in water hyacinth.

This call for action marked the beginning of the cleanup campaign for the Bhairab River in the heart of Jashore town. Armed with bamboo, rope, and hooks, Sheikh Sadia entered the water, soon joined by others. Within a few days, a portion of the river was cleared of water hyacinths, revealing some visible water. This endeavor rekindled discussions about the once-glorious Bhairab River of Jashore.

Dr. Sheikh Sadia, a medical officer from the Health Directorate, was born and brought up in Jashore. As a child, she watched the Bhairab River flow. Her family still rents a house along its banks. Last year, she served in the UN peacekeeping mission in DR Congo as a BCS cadre doctor. On social media, she is known as "Bhairab's Daughter" and "Jashore's Daughter".

An 800-meter campaign in the heart of the town

After returning from Jashore to Dhaka, Sheikh Sadia spoke about her initiative at the Prothom Alo office in Karwan Bazar on 23 November. She described it as the “water hyacinth uprooting” campaign.

Sheikh Sadia stated that a river within a city is crucial for people’s lives and health. However, there seemed to be a kind of neglect among people regarding the river. The idea of whether something could be done at an individual level or whether people could be stirred led her to start this work.

Dr. Sheikh Sadia, a medical officer from the Health Directorate, was born and brought up in Jashore. As a child, she watched the Bhairab River flow. Her family still rents a house along its banks. Last year, she served in the UN peacekeeping mission in DR Congo as a BCS cadre doctor. On social media, she is known as "Bhairab's Daughter" and "Jashore's Daughter".

She added that from 6th to 22nd November, approximately 800 meters or more from Doratana Bridge to the wooden bridge in the town’s heart were cleared of water hyacinths. The removed hyacinths were dumped on nearby land. This spot is quite significant, with a market on one side and a hospital on the other, along with a slaughterhouse. Various wastes, including market and medical waste, have been discarded into the river.

The Bhairab River stretches 133 kilometers from Taherpur in Chowgacha, Jashore, to Rupsa in Khulna. Despite dredging, the natural flow of water is obstructed within the town section. Several bridges, like the Doratana and wooden bridge, being narrow in comparison to the river’s width, hinder the water flow.

According to Sheikh Sadia, removing water hyacinth with bamboo, hooks, and rope is not a large-scale task. It’s basically a symbolic initiative. However, this effort has initiated discussions among people about the river.

Sadia expressed, “I undertook this work out of emotion and love. This has created a stir among people about the river. It has somewhat awakened their conscience. People are recognising the pride of Bhairab in Jashore. Hopefully, a good plan will emerge soon.”

Sheikh Sadia has called upon the people of Jashore to clean the remaining parts of Bhairab. However, she believes that proper planning and modern equipment are necessary for this task.

Family support and the moon on the river

Sheikh Sadia’s father, Sheikh Abdus Samad, is a businessman, and her mother, Rawnak Rayhana, is a homemaker. Her brother, Sheikh Ejazul Mumit, serves as a captain in the army, and her sister, Sheikh Samiya Imrana, studies at BUET.

Sheikh Sadia mentioned that from the start, she had her family’s support for this river cleanup initiative. The trust and confidence her family members had in her work motivated her to continue.

Physician Sheikh Sadia Manowara UshaAs a doctor, when I see a wound or infection, I first try to stop the bleeding. I then clean the wound and look for the source of infection to stop it. Regarding the Bhairab River, I felt that initially removing the water hyacinths was necessary to make the river visible to people.

After posting about it on Facebook, she initially cleared water hyacinths from a small stretch of the riverbank beside her home. She saw the reflection of clouds in that small amount of water. It made her feel that if the whole river were clear, the sky's reflection would be visible in the water, creating a beautiful sight.

On 22 November, she finally saw the moon on that river. The moment when the moonlight fell on water long covered by water hyacinths was special to her.

This doctor recounted, “After working all day, we were soaked in sweat and water. The boat was wet, the bamboo was wet, and our hands and feet were sore. In such a state, the moonlight was shining on the river. It felt like our collective joy was merging with the moonlight on the river.”

The river's wound through a physician’s eyes

Dr. Sheikh Sadia draws insights from her professional experience in taking the initiative to clean up the river. To her, the situation of the Bhairab River appeared similar to a wound or infection.

Sadia described, “As a doctor, when I see a wound or infection, I first try to stop the bleeding. I then clean the wound and look for the source of infection to stop it. Regarding the Bhairab River, I felt that initially removing the water hyacinths was necessary to make the river visible to people.”

She believes the river should have its own colour, with the flow of water, currents, and tides. People need to understand that it is indeed a river.

Drawing from her medical experience, she emphasised the importance of the environment. In hospitals, a patient might receive successive antibiotics for an infection, but eventually, the germs become resistant. Hence, alongside treatment, prevention holds importance.

According to Sheikh Sadia, emphasising prevention extends to working with flowers, birds, rivers, and the environment, as ultimately if the environment isn't healthy, human health won't be either.

Progress with the support of volunteers

Initially, there was a lack of necessary equipment and manpower for the river cleanup. Eventually, along with the general public, representatives from volunteer organisations like "We are Bangladesh" and "BD Clean" joined. Their skills and support made it possible to advance the work.
Sheikh Sadia commented, “Those who cleaned the water hyacinths or supported the river cleanup weren’t actually with me; they stood by Bhairab.”

Many people, after seeing her work’s pictures and videos on social media, are now undertaking similar initiatives. However, Sheikh Sadia issued a word of caution. She believes, although the volunteers working with her had some experience with such risky tasks, it might not be safe for the general public.

She acknowledged the risk she took by entering the water, and advised that those unfamiliar with these kinds of tasks shouldn’t take such risks.

Criticism, threats, yet unyielding

The river cleanup initiative faced criticism on social media. Some people claimed that she was working only to go viral on Facebook.

In response, Sheikh Sadia remarked, “I used to share my creative work, travel stories, delightful moments, time spent with my mother, photography, or writing related to medical science. I never felt the need to do something just to go viral on Facebook.”

In her view, it's easy to criticise standing on the riverbank, but stepping into the water helps realise the enormity of the task. Alongside online criticism, a few people made calls seeming threatening.

However, none of this could deter her. Sheikh Sadia firmly believes that to accomplish something significant, minor fears or criticisms must not be focused on.

She was cautious about financial transactions throughout this initiative. When the State Minister for Energy and Mineral Resources, Aninda Islam Amit, offered to donate Tk 100,000, it was declined.

Sheikh Sadia explained, “Since the work was initiated of my own volition, I was determined from the start that we wouldn't manage any large funds or financial transactions. Those eager to help could provide necessary tools, food, or manpower but were requested not to offer cash to us directly. This was communicated in an open letter to the minister as well.”

Additionally, she talked about seeking government assistance for moving the water hyacinths gathered on the riverbanks.

Sheikh Sadia noted that although she heard that government officials occasionally visited the worksite, she never met them directly.

The deputy commissioner had informed her that two trucks from the municipality would daily remove the water hyacinths, but nothing of that sort was witnessed. No direct communication with anyone concerned was established.

On the future plans for the Bhairab River, Sheikh Sadia expressed, “Even on the day when everyone decides to stop working, I will still contemplate about Bhairab on my own.”

She wishes to see the reflection of the sky, the moonlight glimmering on the river’s water again, and calls upon everyone not to dump waste into the Bhairab River.

*The article, originally published in Prothom Alo print and online editions, has been rewritten in English by Rabiul Islam.

item.title: UN Women and UNHCR deepen collaboration for a more inclusive Rohingya refugee response
item.description:
UN Women and UNHCR today, Thursday, renewed their partnership by signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to make the Rohingya refugee response in Bangladesh more gender-responsive and inclusive by advancing women’s rights, protection, and leadership in the humanitarian response and in decisions that affect their lives.

Signed by Gitanjali Singh, Representative of UN Women, and Ivo Freijsen, Representative of UNHCR, the agreement establishes a framework for cooperation through 2028.

“Rohingya women and girls have shown remarkable resilience in the face of displacement, uncertainty and hardship. Yet they continue to face significant barriers to participation, leadership and opportunities,” said Gitanjali Singh. “Women’s leadership is lifesaving. Upholding the rights and dignity of women and girls, including survivors of sexual violence, means ensuring their voice, choice and safety. We must match our commitments with concrete action and sustained investment to make this a reality for every Rohingya woman and girl.”

“Among the 1.2 million Rohingya refugees living in Bangladesh, more than half are women and girls, and thousands of women already play a vital role in supporting their families and communities,” said Ivo Freijsen. “Refugee women are not only beneficiaries of assistance, but advocates and agents of change. Together with UN Women, we are committed to creating more space for Rohingya women to lead and influence decisions in their communities.”

The collaboration will focus on further integrating gender equality and protection into humanitarian planning and services; increasing women's representation and participation in camp governance and decision-making; enhancing support for Rohingya women-led groups; and expanding opportunities for education, skills development, livelihoods and leadership.

As part of the agreement, UNHCR and UN Women will work with humanitarian actors, government counterparts, refugee volunteers and community leaders to strengthen their capacities on refugee protection and gender equality, challenge harmful gender norms and promote positive masculinities, and jointly advocate for policies and programmes that respond to the needs of women, girls, men and boys.

The signing comes during the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence, a global call for collective action to prevent and respond to violence against women and girls. It also reflects the United Nations' continued commitment to the rights and protection of Rohingya communities.

Following the recent ICJ ruling on The Gambia vs Myanmar, UNHCR and UNWOMEN echo the statement issued by the UN Secretary-General and will continue to stand alongside Rohingya refugees working to uphold their rights, ensure their protection and support efforts towards lasting solutions.

The MoU builds on the long-standing partnership between the two agencies. It supports the Global Compact on Refugees and the Inter-Agency Standing Committee's Gender Equality and Women's Empowerment Agenda.
