item.title: SP Azad arrested, several other police officers under surveillance
item.description:
Police Superintendent (SP) Abul Kalam Azad has been arrested in a crimes against humanity case over the killing of Nuruzzaman Jony, former general secretary of the Khilgaon Thana unit of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD), in what police described at the time as a gunfight.

Since 14 November, two SPs and two additional SPs, including Azad, have been arrested.

The Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) arrested Azad from the In-Service Training Centre in Gazipur on Wednesday.

Speaking to Prothom Alo on Thursday, DMP Additional Commissioner (DB) Md Shafiqul Islam said Azad had been arrested in connection with the Nuruzzaman Jony murder case. He was working at the training centre in Gazipur.

Azad, a native of Jhalakathi, is a 25th batch Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) police cadre officer.

The other three officers arrested are Chattogram Range Reserve Force SP Mohammad Jahangir Alam and Additional SPs Abul Hasan and Md Rakibul Hasan.

Jahangir Alam was arrested on the night of 14 November in a sedition case filed with Panchlaish police station in Chattogram city. The allegations against him include maintaining contact with leaders of the Awami League, whose activities have been banned in the country, and supplying them with confidential information from within the police force.

Additional SP Abul Hasan was arrested in connection with the murder of ruling BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) activist Mokbul Hossain in Dhaka. A Dhaka court ordered him to be sent to jail on Tuesday.

DMP said today that 33rd BCS police cadre Rakibul Hasan would be shown arrested in a murder case filed with Paltan police station in the capital.

Jony abducted from outside prison

On 19 January 2015, Nuruzzaman Jony went to Dhaka Central Jail to visit his younger brother. His family alleged that police picked him up along with one of his associates from outside the prison.

According to the family, the following morning, Jony was shot dead at Khilgaon playground in what police staged as a gunfight. At the time, the Detective Branch claimed that he had been killed in a gunfight.

In September 2024, Jony's father, Yakub Ali, filed a murder case with Khilgaon police station, accusing 62 people. An allegation of Jony's murder was subsequently brought before the International Crimes Tribunal as well.

Following a request from the tribunal, the DB arrested Azad on Wednesday.

Police officers under continued surveillance

Police have stepped up security amid fears of sabotage surrounding ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina's announcement that she would return to the country from India and programmes organised by the Awami League, whose activities have been banned in the country. Surveillance within the police force has also been intensified.

Speaking at a press conference at the Secretariat on Wednesday, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said some officials of law enforcement agencies, including the police, were associated with “fascist forces”.

The government had placed them under close surveillance, he said, adding that action was being taken against several of them.

Several senior police sources told Prothom Alo that some officers had been accused of involvement in crimes committed while performing their duties at their respective workplaces before the mass uprising.

Such allegations have featured in the cases leading to their arrests. However, information about leaks of internal police intelligence and contacts with leaders of the Awami League, whose activities have been banned in the country, has also played a role in the decision to take action against them after such a long interval, the sources said.

Police Headquarters spokesperson and Assistant Inspector General (AIG) Kamarum Munira told Prothom Alo on Wednesday that cases had been filed and departmental action taken against several police personnel on the basis of specific allegations and information.

The activities of others facing similar allegations are also being monitored by intelligence agencies, she added.

item.title: Miss Universe: From Shela to Mahi, who has taken Bangladesh furthest?
item.description:
Bangladesh’s history of participation in Miss Universe, one of the world’s biggest beauty pageants, is relatively short. The country first took part in the competition in 2019. After a gap of several years, a contestant represented Bangladesh on the international stage again in 2024.

In total, four contestants have represented the country in the main Miss Universe competition so far. The latest was actress Samira Khan Mahi, who took part in 2026. However, only one of them has managed to reach the top 30.

Shirin Akter Shela was the first to represent Bangladesh at Miss Universe in 2019. She earned the opportunity to compete internationally after winning the Miss Universe Bangladesh pageant.

Mahi misses out; here are the contestants who made it to the top 30

Tangia Zaman Methila won the Miss Universe Bangladesh crown in 2020 but could not take part in the international competition because of travel restrictions during the Covid-19 pandemic. As a result, Bangladesh had no representative in the competition from 2021 to 2023.

Bangladesh returned to Miss Universe in 2024, represented by Aniqa Alam. Tangia Zaman Methila represented the country again in 2025. She made history by becoming the first Bangladeshi contestant to reach the top 30 at Miss Universe.

She achieved this by competing against contestants from 122 countries. Methila also received strong support in the public vote.

Samira Khan Mahi represented Bangladesh in 2026. She was crowned Miss Universe Bangladesh 2026 at an event in Dhaka on 8 November. She then competed in the 75th Miss Universe pageant, held in Puerto Rico. This year’s competition featured contestants from 116 countries and territories.

Mahi breaks down in tears after seeing Methila at the camp

How are contestants selected for the top 30?

A place in the Miss Universe top 30 does not depend solely on public votes. Before the competition, contestants must demonstrate their abilities to the judges in several rounds.

For the 2026 pageant, four categories were officially considered as part of the evaluation for selecting the top 30: the personal interview, national costume, evening gown and swimsuit rounds.

According to the Miss Universe website, public voting also offered one contestant the opportunity to secure a direct place in the top 30.

Expectations among Bangladeshi viewers were high for Mahi from the outset. Towards the end of the competition, she was leading the People’s Choice vote.

Mahi wears khadi sari in Miss Universe, celebrates motherhood and motherland

The winner of this vote had the chance to earn a direct place in the top 30. However, Mahi did not manage to secure the spot. She lost the lead in the vote about an hour before the final.

In the end, Ecuador’s Dalia Bucaram won the People’s Choice vote and secured a place in the top 30.

At the grand final, held on 25 November, Mahi failed to make the top 30. Her Miss Universe journey therefore ended before the semi-final stage. Of the four contestants who have represented Bangladesh in the international competition, Tangia Zaman Methila remains the only one to have reached the top 30.

Admission will be conducted through five units: Unit A (under the Faculty of Science and the Faculty of Life and Earth Sciences), Unit B (under the Faculties of Arts and Law), Unit C (under the Faculty of Business Studies), Unit D (under the Faculty of Social Sciences) and Unit E (under the Faculty of Fine Arts).

- Unit A (Science and Life and Earth Sciences): Applicants must have a combined GPA of at least 7.00 in SSC and HSC, with a GPA of at least 3.00 in either examination. The application fee is Tk 1,200.

- Unit B (Arts and Law): Applicants must have a combined GPA of at least 6.00, with a GPA of at least 2.75 in either examination. The application fee is Tk 1,200.

- Unit C (Business Studies): Applicants must have a combined GPA of at least 6.50, with a GPA of at least 3.00 in either examination. The application fee is Tk 1,200.

- Unit D (Social Sciences): Applicants must have a combined GPA of at least 6.00, with a GPA of at least 2.75 in either examination. The application fee is Tk 1,200.

item.title: It's not possible to shut down all brick kilns, but the most harmful ones must be closed first: Martin Mattsson
item.description:
The ‘Brick Kiln Tracker’ has been developed using satellite data, machine learning and air-quality modelling to help control pollution from brick kilns in Bangladesh. It can identify how harmful individual brick kilns are to human health. The research was led by Martin Mattsson, Assistant Professor in the Department of Economics at the National University of Singapore. Interview by Partha Shankar Saha.

What motivated you to undertake this research and develop the 'Brick Kiln Tracker’ for Bangladesh? Why do you think brick kiln pollution deserves particular attention in the country’s air pollution crisis?

Martin Mattsson : Bangladesh loses more life expectancy to air pollution than any other country: 5.5 years for the average person (Air Quality Life Index, 2025). Brick kilns are one of the largest sources, particularly in winter, when they operate and the weather traps pollution over the cities. Estimates of the kilns’ share of Dhaka’s fine-particle pollution range from about a tenth, which is my team’s estimate for the winter season, to more than half.

Kiln pollution also deserves attention because it is avoidable: Bangladesh does not need as many fired bricks as it is currently using. Hollow concrete blocks are made from cement, sand and stone chips and harden without being fired, so making them produces no kiln smoke. Concrete blocks are widely used both around the world and in Bangladesh, and switching most construction to using concrete blocks is feasible within just a few years if we start today.

The Tracker uses satellite imagery, machine learning and air-quality modelling. Could you explain how these technologies work together to identify individual brick kilns, classify their technologies and estimate their pollution levels? How accurate and reliable are these estimates?

Martin Mattsson : There are three steps. First, a neural network scans high-resolution satellite images for kilns. We combine its results with earlier kiln maps, and a person then checks every kiln in the imagery, recording its technology (zigzag or fixed-chimney) and whether it operated that season, from signs such as smoke and drying bricks. We then trained another machine learning algorithm to tell the difference between an active and closed kiln from lower-resolution imagery that is updated more frequently. Using this lower-resolution imagery, we update the map with information about which kilns are active every season. So the current tracker is based on which kilns were active in the 2025/26 brick kiln season.

Second, we estimate each kiln’s emissions from how much coal kilns of its type burn, based on our survey of kiln managers, and from field measurements in South Asia of the pollution released per unit of coal. An air quality model then traces where the pollution travels during the brick season. Third, we combine the resulting pollution with population maps and standard estimates of how fine-particle exposure raises mortality to calculate a health harm score for each individual kiln.

The health estimates are modelled, not measured. The largest uncertainty is how much a kiln emits: few studies have measured kiln emissions, and their results differ substantially. The total number of deaths caused by kilns is therefore uncertain. The ranking of kilns is more reliable, because the same assumptions apply to every kiln and the differences between kilns come from location and technology, which we observe well. One limitation is that we assume all kilns of one technology emit the same amount, so a badly run kiln, or one burning dirtier fuel, may do more harm than the tracker shows.

What are the most important findings from your research? How many brick kilns have been identified across Bangladesh, and are there particular regions or districts where the concentration of kilns is especially high?

Martin Mattsson : We have mapped more than 9,000 kilns that have operated at some point since 2010. In the 2025/26 season about 6,000 were active, and more than four in five of these were zigzag kilns. The number of active kilns peaked in 2019 and has fallen by more than a fifth since, with fixed-chimney kilns falling fastest.

The most important finding is that the harm is concentrated: 14 per cent of kilns cause a quarter of the health damage from all kilns, and a third of kilns cause half. Kilns close to and upwind of a large city do the most harm per kiln, because more people breathe their smoke. People in the areas covered by the pilot of our new public tracker, iterbhata.com, can look up each kiln near them and how harmful it is. While we evaluate the pilot, I would rather not single out districts or upazilas outside it.

The current siting rules are a poor guide to this harm. Kilns near schools, hospitals, wetlands or forests are on average about as harmful as other kilns.

Your research estimates the potential health impacts of pollution from individual brick kilns. What are the major health risks associated with this pollution? Can you quantify the potential health burden, particularly in terms of respiratory and cardiovascular diseases and premature deaths?

Martin Mattsson : Kiln smoke contains fine particles (PM2.5) and gases such as sulphur dioxide that form more fine particles in the air. Long-term exposure to fine particles raises the risk of heart disease, stroke, chronic lung disease, lung cancer and lower respiratory infections such as pneumonia.

Our model estimates premature deaths; it does not estimate the larger number of people who fall ill. I prefer not to give a single figure for total deaths, because it depends heavily on assumptions about emissions and the plausible range is wide. Some recent evidence suggests that particles from burning coal are more harmful than the average particle, so our estimates may, if anything, be too low. We are more confident about comparisons: which kilns do the most harm, and how the total has changed. By that measure, the harm from kilns has fallen by about 30% since 2019 as kilns closed or switched to zigzag technology.

How significant is the difference in pollution between zigzag kilns and traditional fixed-chimney kilns? Does adopting zigzag technology necessarily mean that a kiln is environmentally safe, or are there other factors that need to be considered?

Martin Mattsson : The difference is substantial. Per brick, a fixed-chimney kiln emits about twice as much fine-particle pollution as a zigzag kiln, and more than four times as much sulphur dioxide, which forms more fine particles in the air. Fixed-chimney kilns have been banned since 2013, yet about one in six active kilns still uses the technology.

But a zigzag kiln is not safe. It still burns coal and still pollutes. Location matters as much as technology: about four in five of the most harmful kilns in the country are zigzag kilns, because a zigzag kiln upwind of a large city exposes far more people than a fixed-chimney kiln in a sparsely populated area. How well a kiln is run also matters. Converting every fixed-chimney kiln still operating to zigzag would cut the health harm from kilns by less than a tenth. Teaching zigzag kiln owners to operate their kilns more efficiently may reduce their emissions by another 20 per cent. Closing the most harmful fifth of kilns, whatever their technology, would cut the health harm by about a third.

Prothom Alo: Bangladesh has laws and regulations governing brick kilns, but illegal and highly polluting kilns continue to operate. How can this publicly accessible Tracker help government agencies enforce environmental regulations? Could it become an effective tool for holding kiln owners and authorities accountable?

Martin Mattsson : There are two versions of the tracker. Department of Environment officials log in to a version that is designed for government use. The second version is public: iterbhata.com. We are launching it first as a pilot covering about a third of all upazilas, where anyone can see each kiln on a map with its technology and estimated health harm. If the pilot is successful, we plan to expand the public tracker to all of Bangladesh.

On accountability: because the ranking is objective, the Department’s headquarters or the Ministry can check whether each district office is acting against the most harmful kilns. The public tracker lets residents, journalists and local representatives see which kilns near them do the most harm and nudge the authorities to act.

Prothom Alo: Based on your research, what are the three most important actions Bangladesh should take to reduce pollution from brick kilns? Should the country focus on stricter enforcement, cleaner kiln technologies, alternative building materials, or a combination of these approaches?

Martin Mattsson : A combination. First, direct enforcement at the kilns that do the most harm. Since almost every kiln breaks the law, the question is where to start. The tracker gives officials a list of the most harmful kilns, and the officials’ version now covers the whole country. Second, make enforcement against those kilns stick. A small fine rarely stops a kiln. Closures should last, and seasonal satellite updates can show whether a closed kiln has started operating again.

Third, encourage construction companies and public infrastructure projects to use alternatives to traditional fired bricks. Bricks are still the country’s main construction material, so closing all kilns is not realistic in the near term, which is why priorities matter. Over time, alternatives such as hollow concrete blocks should replace fired bricks, and the government can speed this up by meeting its own target of using blocks in public construction.

Furthermore, the government could ban kilns from operating during the worst air pollution season of November, December, and January. That would substantially reduce the health harms that kilns cause.

item.title: 4 killed in Rangpur: Victim’s brother dismisses theft motive as ‘flimsy excuse’
item.description:
Four members of a family, including retired Rangpur Zilla School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, were murdered after they caught two men breaking into their home to commit theft, police have said.

The two accused, Siddhartha Das and Mugdha Das, were responsible for the killings, according to a charge sheet submitted to the Rangpur Metropolitan Magistrate’s Court on Thursday morning.

However, Gopinath Chakraborty, the victim’s elder brother and the plaintiff in the case, has rejected the police explanation and the findings presented in the charge sheet.

Addressing a press conference, held at the conference room of the Rangpur Metropolitan Police Commissioner’s Office at 1:00 pm today, RMP Commissioner Md Mahbubur Rashid said Siddhartha Das and Mugdha Das had gone to Ganapati’s house intending to steal money and gold ornaments, having learnt that valuables were kept there.

While waiting on the roof of the house, they were spotted by Ganapati Chakraborty. When he tried to stop them, they killed him first. They then murdered the other three members of his family, the commissioner said.

He added that the two accused had given confessional statements before a court under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).

4 murders in Rangpur: Suspects’ DNA found on date seed, cucumber, towel

Some of the stolen gold ornaments had also been recovered on the basis of information provided by them, the RMP commissioner added.

At the press conference, Deputy Commissioner of the RMP Detective Branch (DB) Sanatan Chakraborty outlined the planning and details of the killings.

He said the murders were committed primarily with the intention of theft, with the perpetrators using a gamchha (traditional cotton towel), rope and physical force.

2 suspects to undergo dope tests, questions about killings will be answered: Police

The DB official further said Siddhartha Das and Mugdha Das had gone to the rooftop of the house to commit theft. There were rumours in the neighbourhood that Ganapati Chakraborty had withdrawn Tk 5-6 million from his bank account after retiring and kept the money at home.

Ganapati’s wife, Pritilata Chakraborty, was also frequently seen leaving the house wearing expensive jewellery. Having heard and observed these things, their neighbours Siddhartha and Mugdha planned to break into the house and steal the valuables.

When their attempt was thwarted, the two men first killed Ganapati, followed by his wife and their two children, the DB official said.

4 murders in Rangpur: Police commissioner gives new account of crime scene, timing and motive

At the press conference, police said 31 types of samples had been collected from the crime scene on 31 August and 1 September and sent to the Criminal Investigation Department’s (CID) forensic laboratory for examination. Investigators also recorded statements from 53 witnesses.

DNA belonging to Mugdha Das was detected on a date seed, while Siddhartha Das’s DNA was found on a piece of cucumber. DNA from both accused was detected on a cigarette butt.

4 murders in Rangpur: How unjustified the questions raised about information provided by police?

Furthermore, only Mugdha Das’s DNA was found on samples taken from the gamchha wrapped around the neck of the deceased Pritilata Chakraborty.

DB official Sanatan Chakraborty said an analysis of the DNA test results, recovered evidence, confessional statements and witness testimonies had provided clear evidence of the involvement of Siddhartha Das and Mugdha Das in the killings.

However, Gopinath Chakraborty remains unconvinced by the police account and the charge sheet.

4 killed in Rangpur: Funerals held side by side

“Claiming that all four were murdered for money is a flimsy excuse. Someone more powerful is behind this. We have maintained from the beginning that the two men could not have killed all four. We demanded a fair investigation and the identification of the actual perpetrators. But our concerns were not given due consideration,” he said.

On the night of 22 August, police recovered the bodies of Ganapati Chakraborty, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty and their two children, Agami Chakraborty and Ayush Chakraborty, from their home in Machhuapara in Rangpur city.

The following day, Gopinath Chakraborty filed a murder case with Kotwali police station against unidentified persons.

Horrific murders one after another across the country

Initially, Milon Chatterjee, an inspector (investigation) at the police station, was appointed as the investigation officer. On the next day, 24 August, the case was transferred to the Detective Branch of Rangpur Metropolitan Police. DB Inspector Jinnat Ali subsequently led the investigation.

item.title: Murder, suicide, or accident—what the investigation into Tahsif Souri's death has revealed so far
item.description:
Murder, suicide or an accident—even a month after the death of former Bangladesh Air Force officer KM Tahsif Souri, this question remains unanswered. The Naval police are investigating all three possibilities after his body was recovered from the Turag River.

Investigators are searching for answers to where Tahsif went after leaving his house, who was with him and what happened on the riverbank. They have recorded statements and testimonies from at least 40 people and are examining evidence from four key locations. However, the full autopsy report has yet to be received.

The naval police, the investigating agency in the case, said Tahsif's father, AKM Enayetul Karim filed a murder case. His junior friend Ahmed Shahriar Dip (23) and a young woman known to him have been arrested in the case and are now in jail. However, investigators have yet to determine whether Tahsif's death was a murder, suicide or accident.

The investigation of the case is being supervised by the head of Naval Police and Additional Inspector General of Police (Additional IGP) Md. Rezaul Karim. He told Prothom Alo that the incident of Tahsif''s death is being investigated from three perspectives.

Murder, suicide and accident—all possibilities are being taken into consideration. Once answers to all questions are found, the results of the investigation will be disclosed through a press conference. Following that, a police report will be submitted to the court.

Police probing four locations

According to Naval Police sources, investigators are tracing Tahsif's movements before his death. Four locations have emerged as particularly important: his residence in Uttara, a hotel, a bar and the Tongi Mazar Road slum area along the Turag River.

Investigators are trying to find out what happened at these places, who was present and whether their accounts match other evidence. They are also looking into whether there were any other incidents or connections beyond these four locations.

Investigating officials say they are checking for any inconsistencies between the information gathered regarding Tahsif's movements before and after his death and the roles of the individuals involved. They do not want to reach a conclusion based on a single piece of information.

According to Naval Police sources, statements and testimonies of at least 40 people have been recorded so far. Most of them have been interrogated.

Investigators are cross-checking the information obtained from their accounts against other evidence. When a statement raises multiple issues, each needs to be verified. Several more people may need to be questioned, and various pieces of information require further scrutiny.

The source said some of the information needed to establish a definitive sequence of events remains incomplete. Investigators are also working on several sensitive aspects of the case. These details are being collected and verified.

Full autopsy report yet to be received

An inquest report was prepared after Tahsif's body was recovered. His autopsy was subsequently conducted at the morgue of Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College. The inquest report noted that no visible injury marks were found on his body.

Nashat Jabin, assistant professor of forensic medicine at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College, told Prothom Alo that samples from Tahsif's stomach, liver, kidneys and blood had been sent to a laboratory for testing. The full autopsy report will be prepared once the laboratory results are received. After that, the actual cause of death could be determined, she said.

However, the physician did not comment on whether there were any injury marks on Tahsif's body.

Abdullah Al Mamun, superintendent of police of the Naval Police's Dhaka region and the officer supervising the investigation, told Prothom Alo that Tahsif's autopsy report has not yet reached their hands.

The Naval Police considers the autopsy report important in determining the cause of death. However, investigators do not want to conclude the investigation solely on the basis of the report. They are also collecting and analysing information about the circumstances before and after the incident, statements from those involved and other circumstantial evidence.

An investigation source further said the autopsy report is an important part of the probe, but establishing the actual cause of death also required determining what happened before and after the incident. Some information has already been obtained, and its authenticity is being verified.

Naval Police also verifying media statements

The Naval Police are also following reports published in the media and statements made on social media concerning Tahsif's death.

A senior Naval Police officer involved in the investigation, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said reports published in various media outlets were yielding information that could be useful to the investigation. Investigators are also following interviews given by individuals on Facebook and statements made on television talk shows.

The official said that listening to the statements of some participants in talk shows gave the impression that they might have some clues or information about the incident. Some of them were even contacted, but they did not respond. These information and statements are being verified in the interest of the investigation.

Body recovered from river the following day

According to sources involved in the investigation, on 27 October, Tahsif left from beneath their residence at the RAJUK Apartment Project in Uttara Sector 18 on a motorcycle with Dip. He later went to a bar in Uttara Sector 13 with a young woman he knew previously. Dip was also with them at the bar.

According to investigators, Tahsif had a disagreement with the woman at the bar. About an hour later, he left the bar and dropped her off in front of her residence on his motorcycle. Tahsif and Dip then went to the Tongi Mazar Road slum area.

During questioning, Dip told police officers that they saw two police personnel in uniform there and ran in opposite directions. Dip said he hid near a pillar belonging to the Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority (BIWTA) on the bank of the Turag River.

According to Dip, the two police personnel later approached him and questioned him. After he told them he had come with Tahsif, they did not pursue the conversation and told him to leave. Dip claimed he did not see Tahsif again afterwards.

However, at 1:35am, Tahsif sent a voice message to his mother's mobile phone, saying, “I'm coming, I've set off.”

Four minutes later, at 1:39am, Dip called the caretaker of their rented residence in Mohammadpur and said he would be late returning home. Dip returned home around 2:30am.

The Naval Police have collected information about the events of that night and CCTV footage. Several individuals have also provided videos showing people moving around the Tongi Mazar Road slum area to the Naval Police. These videos and statements from those involved are being verified.

An investigation source said an eight-member police patrol team was in the Tongi Mazar Road slum area at the time of the incident. The officers have also been questioned in connection with Tahsif's death.

Body recovered from river the following day

On the afternoon of 28 October, the Naval Police received a report through the National Emergency Service 999 that an unidentified body was floating in the Turag River near Rajabari Ghat in Uttarkhan.

The body was initially recovered as unidentified. His identity was later established through an iPhone found in the pocket of his pyjama. He was former Air Force Flight Lieutenant KM Tahsif Souri (28).

Two days after the body was recovered, on the night of 30 October, his father, AKM Enayetul Karim, filed a murder case with Uttarkhan Police Station. No one was named as a suspect in the case.

The Naval Police was assigned to investigate the case. Before that, the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) had conducted a shadow investigation into the incident. They took Tahsif's junior friend Ahmed Shahriar Dip into custody. Based on information provided by Dip, Tahsif's motorcycle was later recovered from the Tongi Mazar slum area.

Investigators said Dip and the young woman who had joined them at the bar were detained by the Naval Police. They were subsequently shown arrested in the murder case filed over the recovery of Tahsif's body. Both are now in jail.

Investigation considers three possibilities

The murder case filed by Tahsif's father, Enayetul Karim, alleges that Tahsif was killed and his body dumped in the river.

However, an investigation source said investigators had yet to obtain all the evidence needed to reach a definitive conclusion either for or against murder. They are examining testimonies, evidence and the circumstances surrounding the incident to determine which of the three possibilities—murder, suicide or accident—is the actual cause.

Investigators said they are checking for inconsistencies in the information gathered about Tahsif's movements before his death, his presence at various locations and the roles of those involved. The actual cause of death must be established after examining all the evidence, they said.

Father wants investigation handed over to CID or PBI

Tahsif's father, AKM Enayetul Karim, told Prothom Alo that he and Tahsif's mother have not been in good health since their son's death. He believes that his son had been murdered. However, he does not know whether Dip and the young woman in jail are involved in this incident, nor has he been informed of any investigation results.

Enayetul Karim said it would have been better if the investigation of the murder case had been handed over to the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) or PBI. He hopes that investigators will find out who is involved in this incident.

item.title: DU takes administrative action against six teachers, including former VC
item.description:
Dhaka University (DU) authorities have taken administrative action against six faculty members, including former vice-chancellor Professor Dr ASM Maksud Kamal.
The university's Syndicate has decided to temporarily suspend two teachers, asked two others—including the former vice-chancellor—to appear in person before the registrar within seven working days, and decided to issue formal charge sheets against two more faculty members.
Professor Dr Mohammed Almujaddade Alfasane, pro-vice-chancellor (administration) of Dhaka University, confirmed the decisions to Bangla Tribune on Wednesday afternoon.
The decisions were taken at a Syndicate meeting, the university's highest policy-making body, held on Monday night.
The two teachers placed under temporary suspension are Professor Mushfiqur Rahman of the Department of Accounting and Information Systems and Lecturer Azhar Uddin Bhuiyan of the Department of Law.
The action was taken because they had been staying abroad without university authorisation. The Syndicate has also formed separate investigation committees to examine their cases.
“They have been temporarily suspended in accordance with university regulations. Separate investigation committees have also been formed to look into their respective cases,” Professor Alfasane said.
The Syndicate has directed former vice-chancellor Professor Dr ASM Maksud Kamal and Lecturer Shahrima Tanzin Orni of the Department of Law to appear in person before the university registrar within seven working days.
The directive follows their failure to resume their duties after their leave expired.
Professor Alfasane said the university had asked the respective departments to provide information about their whereabouts, but they could not furnish any details.
“Consequently, the Syndicate has ordered them to appear in person before the registrar to report,” he said.
The Syndicate has also decided to issue formal charge sheets against Professor Shabnam Jahan of the Department of Management and Professor Kamal Uddin of the Department of Psychology.
The allegations against them include their roles during the July mass uprising and alleged misconduct towards students and fellow faculty members.
University sources said a fact-finding committee had been formed to investigate the allegations. After the committee found them substantiated, the Syndicate decided at Monday's meeting to prepare formal charge sheets.
Professor Alfasane said further action in the matter would be taken at the next Syndicate meeting.

item.title: Two years since lawyer Alif's murder, father hopes to see justice
item.description:
Two years have passed since the murder of Saiful Islam Alif, a lawyer and assistant public prosecutor in Chittagong, but the trial has yet to reach a conclusion. His father says he hopes to live long enough to see justice delivered for his son.
Alif was hacked and beaten to death near the Chittagong court premises on November 26, 2024.
The court has accepted a charge sheet against 37 people, including Chinmoy Krishna Das, spokesperson for the Sanatani Jagaran Jote. Of the accused, 27 have been arrested and are in custody, while 10 remain at large.
Frustrated by the delay, Alif's family and colleagues have renewed their demand for justice. The Chittagong District Bar Association has announced a human chain and protest programme on the court premises. His family has also submitted a memorandum to the deputy commissioner, seeking the transfer of the case to a Speedy Trial Tribunal.
On November 26, 2024, Chinmoy Krishna Das, who had been arrested in Dhaka on sedition charges, was brought before a Chittagong court. After the court rejected his bail application, violence broke out in the court area.
According to the account provided, members of Iskcon attacked several structures, including the Courthill Jame Mosque. A confrontation then erupted between Iskcon members and local lawyers and litigants.
During the violence, Alif was hacked and beaten to death in front of Rangam Convention Hall. The attackers reportedly danced on his body after the killing.
Alif's father, Jamal Uddin, filed a case with Kotwali Police Station, naming 31 people as accused.
On July 1, 2025, the investigating officer, former assistant commissioner of the metropolitan police (Kotwali) Mahfuzur Rahman, submitted a charge sheet naming 37 people, with Chinmoy Krishna Das listed as the prime accused. The court accepted the charge sheet on August 25, 2025.
The other accused named in the charge sheet are Chandan Das Methor, Ripon Das, Rajib Bhattacharya, Shubho Kanti Das, Aman Das, Bunja, Ranab, Bidhan, Bikash, Ramit Prakash Das, Rumit Das, Nayan Das, Omkar Das, Bishal, Lala Das, Samir, Sohel Das, Shiv Kumar, Biglal, Parash, Ganesh, Om Das, Popy, Ajay, Debi Charan, Deb, Joy, Lala Methor, Durlabh Das, Sumit Das, Sonu Das, Saku Das, Bhajan, Ashik, Shahit, Shiba Das and Dwip Das.
Speaking to Bangla Tribune on Wednesday afternoon, Jamal Uddin said: “My son was murdered in broad daylight, in full public view. I will never get him back. I am getting old; I only hope to live long enough to see justice served for my son’s murder. I demand appropriate punishment for those who killed him.”
Assistant Public Prosecutor Md Raihanul Wazed Chowdhury, the lawyer for the case, said the court had accepted the charge sheet against 37 accused. Of them, 27 had been arrested, while 10 remained at large.
He said the charge sheet listed 49 witnesses, but only four had testified so far.
The plaintiff had submitted an application to the Chittagong deputy commissioner seeking the transfer of the case to a Speedy Trial Tribunal, but the request had not yet been granted, he added.
Aminur Rashid, assistant commissioner of police (Public Relations) at Chittagong Metropolitan Police, said efforts were under way to arrest the remaining accused.
“We are actively searching for the 10 accused who remain at large,” he said.

item.title: PM joins opening of National Livestock Week
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday joined the inaugural ceremony of the National Livestock Week-2026 as the chief guest.
The program is being held at the old Trade Fair Ground in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar in the capital, Prime Minister's Deputy Press Secretary Jahidul Islam Rony said.
The Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock and the Department of Livestock Services jointly organised this year's event under the theme "Building the Nation through Export-oriented Livestock, Bangladesh First".
On the occasion, a three-day livestock fair and exhibition is being held at the venue, featuring 64 stalls and six pavilions.
The prime minister will distribute the National Livestock Awards among 23 recipients in eight categories in recognition of their contributions to the development and advancement of the livestock sector.
The National Livestock Week will be observed across all districts and upazilas of the country from Thursday until November 28 through various programs.

item.title: The institutional failure behind graduate unemployment
item.description:
There is a weird waiting room in Bangladesh where nobody has an appointment, nobody knows when a name will be called, and nobody is sure the door will open.
Its occupants are young, educated. They have studied and competed, only to discover that the labour market has a condition they cannot satisfy: Experience. They need a job to gain experience, but need experience to get a job. The waiting room grows as the economy claims to progress.
This is not merely the disappointment of graduates. It is the story of a country better at producing qualifications than organizing opportunities.
A recent study by the Power and Participation Research Center (PPRC) puts youth unemployment among people aged 15 to 29 at 8.07%. The rate rises to 13.5% for bachelor's degree holders and 20.4% for female graduates. Of the country's 2.62 million unemployed people, 885,000 are university graduates.
Even those who find work often enter an insecure world: 92.7% of working young people are employed in the informal sector. A degree no longer reliably signals a route into economic independence.
The familiar explanation is that graduates lack the skills employers need. Curricula can be disconnected from industry, practical learning uneven, and communication and technological abilities underdeveloped. But the skills argument has become a convenient hiding place for systemic failure.
It asks why young people are not ready for work without asking why workplaces will not help them become ready. Employers advertise entry-level jobs requiring experience; universities celebrate graduation without meaningful professional exposure; training centres issue certificates whose value employers rarely test. Everyone produces an output, but nobody owns the transition.
A functioning labour market needs more than graduates on one side and vacancies on the other. It needs a bridge: Employers willing to train, institutions aware of local demand, banks prepared to finance viable ideas, and public agencies that make enterprise possible.
This is the missing middle in Bangladesh's employment story. Policies announce targets and individuals show initiative, but the organizations connecting ambition with opportunity remain fragmented or inaccessible. People are told to become employable, while the institutions responsible for employment are rarely held accountable.
Consider the first-job paradox. A graduate cannot arrive with the experience of someone who has spent years in an industry. Experience must be built, and that requires employers to accept some risk and invest in training.
Paid internships, apprenticeships, supervised placements, and industry-linked university projects should be essential parts of education, with real responsibilities. Employers must also distinguish specialist vacancies from genuine entry-level roles.
A first job should be a starting point, not a test applicants are structurally unable to pass. Universities should assess applied knowledge, not just examination performance.
The waiting room is even more crowded for women. A female graduate may have the same qualifications as a male colleague but face a narrower geography of opportunity.
Unsafe transport, inadequate childcare, harassment, discriminatory recruitment, and unpaid care expectations can turn an apparently open vacancy into an inaccessible one. The 20.4% unemployment rate among female graduates cannot be reduced to individual skills or confidence.
Entrepreneurship schemes are equally inadequate if women seeking loans are asked for property documents they do not own or a husband's signature. Banks must assess business viability rather than reproduce inequality through lending procedures.
For young people who want to create jobs rather than wait for them, the route is hardly easier. Starting a small enterprise can mean navigating registration, licences, taxation, bank requirements, and repeated visits to public offices. When 80% of young people report delays and bribery in accessing government services, administrative friction becomes a tax on initiative, paid in time and money.
A young entrepreneur may have a sound idea but no land for collateral, no credit history or influential connection. The state praises innovation while its procedures make the first step prohibitively expensive. Simplified registration, transparent timelines, accessible credit, and accountable one-stop services would matter more than another startup slogan.
The contradiction is visible beyond major cities. Regions possess assets that could support local jobs if the missing links were built. Rajshahi produces mangoes, but inadequate storage and processing allow value to disappear after harvest. Noakhali grows soybeans, while limited processing restricts the benefits retained locally. Underused space at hi-tech parks raises a basic question: Why build infrastructure without ensuring that businesses, workers, and investment are ready to occupy it?
This calls for a different way of measuring development. A district should not be judged only by roads, buildings, training centres or industrial facilities announced. It should also be judged by local value addition, sustainable jobs, post-training employment, and women's participation.
Local governments, universities, employers, banks and training providers should map their area's economic possibilities. Their performance should be measured through job placement, retention, wage progression, business survival and access to finance, not seminars held or certificates issued. Public incentives should reward firms that train and retain first-time workers, rather than those that merely promise to do so.
The informal economy deserves equal attention. It provides livelihoods for millions and cannot be formalized overnight. But the fact that 92.7% of working youth are employed informally should make policy-makers reconsider what they celebrate as job creation.
Someone without predictable income, written terms, paid leave, insurance or protection against arbitrary dismissal may be employed statistically and insecure in practice. Freelancers and platform workers need fair payment, banking access, and social protection. Formalization should not bury small businesses in paperwork. It should make decent work easier to achieve and sustain.
Nor should Bangladesh assume that economic growth will eventually solve the problem. Growth can coexist with graduate unemployment when investment concentrates in sectors generating few jobs. The demographic advantage is not a permanent asset waiting to be collected. It is a window that can narrow.
A young population becomes an economic dividend only when education, investment, technology, enterprise, and labour institutions work together. Otherwise, a generation of potential contributors risks becoming a generation of postponed lives.
The consequences extend beyond household income. Long unemployment delays independence and family responsibilities, drains confidence and weakens the belief that merit offers a route forward. Families that sacrificed to educate their children may discover that a degree brings neither mobility nor security. Repeatedly closed doors can turn frustration into distrust of institutions and public promises. The loss is not confined to an unemployed individual. It includes resources invested in education, productive capacity left unused and the credibility of a development model that measures progress without asking who gets to participate.
Bangladesh does not need to tell its young people to wait patiently, collect another certificate or become entrepreneurs alone. It needs to make the waiting room smaller.
Employers must open genuine entry routes, universities connect learning with practice, banks recognise viable enterprise beyond traditional collateral, and public agencies treat transparency and time as obligations. That should be the measure of progress, not promises.
Young people are not asking the country to guarantee every ambition. They are asking for a fair chance to begin. A nation that teaches its children to prepare for the future must build a future in which their preparation has somewhere to go.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he is teaching at IUBAT.

item.title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?
item.description:
The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, the central role of Nvidia in the US-China AI competition, and the US economy’s reliance on the AI boom might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?
The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: Central processing units, or CPUs.
GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering.
As a researcher of high-performance computing and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier:
GPUs vs CPUs
The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.
A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion, or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.
From pretty pictures to AI data centres
Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.
In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.
The second major shift occurred when AlexNet, a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs.
AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.
Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.
Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.
AI takes off
In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer, a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.
The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including US-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centres composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.
These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable, and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code, and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.
Nvidia’s GPUs dominate the AI market, but rival companies developing other chips are trying to knock Nvidia off its throne.
AI ‘arms race’
Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the US government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centres require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.
The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.
Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry.
Jeffrey Young is Principal Research Scientist, Partnership for an Advanced Computing Environment, Georgia Institute of Technology. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license.

item.title: Fire at Lotto warehouse in Sherpur
item.description:
A fire at a warehouse of Italian footwear brand Lotto in Sherpur town on Wednesday gutted a large quantity of shoes and damaged an adjacent two-storey building.
The fire broke out around noon at the warehouse in the Khorompur area of the town.
Firefighters from Sherpur Fire Service rushed to the spot and brought the flames under control after nearly an hour of effort.
Although the quick response helped save nearby shops and houses from major damage, a large quantity of shoes stored in the warehouse was gutted, while the adjacent building suffered extensive damage.
Building owner Adil Mahmud Uzzal said he noticed earlier in the morning that someone had disconnected the electricity supply to his residence, suspecting foul play.
Uzzal Sheel, in-charge of Lotto's Sherpur outlet, said they had goods worth around Tk60 lakh in the showroom and warehouse combined.
He estimated the initial losses from the fire at around Tk25 lakh, adding that the actual amount could be determined after an audit.
Atiqur Rahman, deputy director of Sherpur Fire Service, said the cause of the fire would be known after an investigation.
Sherpur Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge Khokon Chandra Ghosh visited the spot.

item.title: RMG entrepreneurs welcome new wage structure despite implementation challenges
item.description:
Garment industry entrepreneurs have welcomed the newly announced wage structure for readymade garment (RMG) workers, describing its implementation as challenging while pledging to enforce it from December 1.
Welcoming the government's initiative to form the Minimum Wage Board and announce the new wages within the shortest possible time, they said the revised structure would play an important role in meeting workers' expectations.
The entrepreneurs said although the wage hike would put some pressure on the industry considering its capacity, production costs and business realities, implementing the government-declared wages in compliance with the country's laws was their responsibility.
Executive President of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) Fazle Shamim Ehsan told BSS that the newly announced wages were higher than the expectations of ordinary workers.
Although the decision would create some difficulties for factory owners, he welcomed it, saying entrepreneurs must comply with the wages fixed under the country's laws to continue doing business.
He expressed disappointment over the continuation of workers' movements even after the announcement of the minimum wages and hoped that workers would accept the government-declared pay structure and return to work soon.
He also said the owners would implement the new wages from December 1.
A K M Shaheed Reza , chairman of garment and textile manufacturing company Reza Group and former director of the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FBCCI), said wages for workers across different grades had increased by 36 to 43 percent under the new structure, making its implementation challenging for entrepreneurs.
However, he said they viewed the development positively.
He described the government's initiative to form the Minimum Wage Board and announce the new wages within a short time as commendable, adding that the process could have started earlier.
He said entrepreneurs appreciated the promptness and sincerity shown by the concerned authorities.
Shaheed Reza said today's entrepreneurs were keen to build a worker-friendly industry and, therefore, viewed the wage increase positively.
However, he noted that the new wage structure had brought the wages of Bangladeshi garment workers close to those in India and Pakistan, creating a new competitive challenge for the industry.
FBCCI Administrator Md Fazlul Haque said they welcomed the announcement of the minimum wages, which were higher than the expectations of many.
However, he said incidents of workers taking to the streets even after the wage announcement in some places needed to be examined carefully.
He said it is necessary to investigate whether any third party is instigating such developments, stressing that the situation should be handled with utmost caution.
He also pointed out that the financial condition of many factories is so difficult that even paying workers' salaries and allowances had become challenging.
Despite these constraints, he said entrepreneurs would implement the new wage structure from December 1.
The entrepreneurs stressed that maintaining a stable working environment alongside implementing the new wage structure was essential for the industry.
They said mutual cooperation and responsible conduct by workers and owners would help sustain production, employment and export growth in the sector.

item.title: MFS account locks leave Gopalganj customers stranded
item.description:
Customers in Gopalganj are facing severe disruption to mobile financial services (MFS), including bKash and Nagad, after a large number of accounts were temporarily blocked over suspected suspicious transactions.
The restrictions have left many users unable to withdraw or send money or make payments, with funds in their accounts inaccessible. The disruption has also affected people of the district living elsewhere in the country.
Most local bKash distributors and service points remained closed on Thursday amid fears of attacks and vandalism by frustrated customers.
Two local area managers of bKash and Nagad told Dhaka Tribune that more than 50% of customers were receiving messages saying their accounts had been locked. Some users said the problems began on Wednesday, without prior notice.
Messages sent from “bKashNotice” informed customers that their accounts had been temporarily suspended under MFS regulations. Customer care representatives reportedly cited suspicious or unethical transactions but did not specify which transactions had triggered the restrictions.
According to conversations with distribution house officials, agents and others who wished to remain anonymous, mobile financial services transactions through agents across the district’s five upazilas amount to at least Tk20 crore a day.
At around 5:30pm, the distribution house on the third floor of Munshi Market in Gopalganj town was found open, with transactions taking place at its cash counter.
Speaking to this correspondent, the head of the distribution house, Sheikh Mujahidul Islam, said mobile financial services, including bKash, Nagad, Upay and Rocket, had been temporarily suspended across Gopalganj district by the government.
He said dealers, agents or service providers should not be held responsible for the disruption.
A local bKash agent said around 30-40% of accounts remained operational. Shakil, an agent in the Kachabazar area, said customers were crowding outlets seeking help, but agents had been unable to resolve the problem despite contacting the head office.
Small and medium-sized businesses have also been affected, as many rely on MFS platforms to receive payments, purchase goods and pay suppliers.
Local distributor Imam Faruk said most accounts had been temporarily restricted in connection with the lockdown situation in Gopalganj. He hoped services would resume from December 1, adding that outlets had been closed to avoid customers' anger.
The disruption follows violence, vandalism and arson in Gopalganj on November 10, when attacks on vehicles, police stations and government installations worsened the security situation. Accounts have reportedly been restricted since then over suspected suspicious transactions.
Tea seller Sazzad Sheikh, from Power House intersection, said he was unable to send Tk7,000 to his father to buy rice seeds as the Boro cultivation season begins. A prolonged disruption, he feared, could delay seed purchases and affect farming.
Tamanna Parvin said she could not send money to her son, who studies in Rajshahi, because of the service disruption. She added that the restrictions had also raised concerns over paying for emergency services and medical treatment.
bKash user Shakil Ahmed said Tk65,000 was stuck in his personal account, leaving him unable to make or receive payments and disrupting his work. He also runs bKash, Nagad and Rocket agent services beneath Trust Bank in the New Market area. While his agent account remained active, his personal account was blocked.
Several bKash agents, speaking on condition of anonymity, said hundreds of thousands of taka belonging to them were also stuck in the service. They urged authorities to investigate and act against accounts linked to specific allegations while keeping ordinary customers' services operational.
Tazul Islam Molla, owner of Tinni Store, which provides bKash, Nagad, Rocket and Upay services, said around 150 customers usually made transactions at his outlet daily, most of them through bKash. Of about 100 customers who visited between Thursday morning and 4:30pm, only 10 could complete transactions. All 10 were from outside the district, he said, adding that the bKash distributor had also suspended cash distribution that day.
Gopalganj Chamber of Commerce and Industry General Secretary Sheikh Masudur Rahman called for restoring services for regular customers while taking action against accounts involved in suspicious transactions.
Gopalganj Deputy Commissioner and Superintendent of Police could not be reached for comment despite repeated phone calls.
bKash Head of Corporate Communications Shamsuddin Haider Dalim said accounts could be temporarily suspended when suspicious transactions are detected under MFS regulations. Their status would be decided after investigations and verification in line with regulatory instructions.
Nagad spokesperson Muhammad Zahidul Islam said the company had not suspended services in any particular district. He said action against accounts linked to suspicious transactions was taken through the regular process following information shared with the Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit.
Bangladesh Bank spokesperson and Executive Director Arief Hossain Khan said the central bank could order the suspension of bank or MFS accounts after receiving information about suspicious transactions. He confirmed that account restrictions in Gopalganj were imposed in response to such transactions.

item.title: Soybean oil prices raised by Tk3 per litre
item.description:
The government has increased soybean oil prices by Tk3 per litre, citing rising international prices, higher import costs and the country's overall supply situation.
Under the revised rates, bottled soybean oil will cost Tk207 per litre, up from Tk204, while loose soybean oil will be sold at Tk188 per litre, compared to Tk185 previously. The price of loose palm oil, however, remains unchanged at Tk166 per litre.
The decision was taken at a meeting held at the Ministry of Commerce's conference room on Thursday afternoon to review the country's overall edible oil supply situation. Commerce Minister Khandaker Abdul Muktadir chaired the meeting.
Mohammad Kamal Hossain, the ministry's public relations officer, said the price of a five-litre bottle of soybean oil had also been raised from Tk1,000 to Tk1,015.
At the meeting, the Bangladesh Trade and Tariff Commission presented a report detailing the country's existing edible oil stocks, international and domestic market prices, opening of letters of credit (LCs), and overall import situation.
After reviewing the report and assessing global and domestic market conditions, the meeting unanimously approved the price adjustment.
Representatives of the Bangladesh Vegetable Oil Refiners and Vanaspati Manufacturers Association said edible oil prices were last adjusted on September 2. Since then, international prices of soybean and palm oil have risen, while domestic prices have remained unchanged, making it increasingly difficult to maintain normal import and supply levels.
With Ramadan approaching, the association called for a fresh price adjustment in line with international market rates and prevailing import costs to ensure adequate stocks and uninterrupted supplies of edible oil across the country.
The meeting also decided to issue necessary directives to businesses concerned to maintain normal market supplies.
The Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection and district administrations were instructed to take legal action against artificial shortages, illegal stockpiling and the sale of edible oil above government-fixed prices.
Bangladesh Trade and Tariff Commission Chairman Nasir-Ud-Doula, Commerce Ministry Additional Secretary Khadija Nazneen, who is performing the routine duties of the secretary, and representatives of relevant government agencies and business associations attended the meeting.

item.title: Police box, land office set ablaze in Chittagong
item.description:
A police box and a room at a land office were targeted in separate arson incidents in Chittagong within hours of each other, police said.
The incidents took place late Wednesday and early Thursday. No one was inside either facility when the fires were set, and no casualties were reported.
At around 5am on Thursday, a fire was set at the Barapole police box under Halishahar Police Station, damaging part of its window. Police brought the situation under control before the flames could spread.
Halishahar Police Station Officer-in-Charge Zainal Abedin Mondal said police intervention prevented major damage. Normal operations at the box continued, and officers were on alert while efforts to identify and arrest those involved remained underway.
Earlier, at around 11:30pm on Wednesday, a curtain beside a window in a room at the Uttar Kattali land office under Pahartali Police Station was set on fire.
Pahartali Police Station OC Nurul Absar said the office's main gate was locked at the time. Police and fire service personnel reached the scene, and firefighters extinguished the blaze after police broke the lock and opened the gate.
Chittagong has seen similar attacks on police facilities in recent days. On November 19, a traffic police box at Saltgola Crossing under Bandar Police Station was vandalised and set on fire during the activities-banned Awami League's announced lockdown program.
On November 17, another traffic police box in Muradpur was targeted, but the fire did not spread inside because its windows were closed.

item.title: Fire, terror damage hundred crore taka’s asset in Gopalganj
item.description:
A series of violent attacks across Gopalganj between November 10 and 25 damaged nearly 100 houses and business establishments, three lawmakers’ residences, police stations, vehicles and public institutions, causing losses estimated at several hundred crore taka, according to a district administration record.
The record attributes the incidents to leaders and activists of the activities-banned Awami League and its affiliated organisations. At least 10 law enforcement vehicles were set on fire, while another 15 vehicles were torched or vandalised. Two police stations were attacked and set ablaze, and a hospital was also damaged.
At least 15 business establishments owned by members of minority communities were vandalised. BNP offices at 15-20 locations and Grameen Bank branches at eight to 10 locations were also attacked or set on fire.
The violence affected all upazilas, with the largest number of incidents recorded on November 19. Tungipara saw some of the earliest attacks, while Gopalganj Sadar experienced damage to a hospital, a lawmaker’s residence, shops, vehicles and a government office.
The first incidents were reported on November 10, when banners and festoons were torn down and a Jubo Dal office was attacked in Tungipara. A police vehicle was also vandalised and set on fire. In Gopalganj Sadar, a cargo truck and a food-delivery vehicle were torched, while shops were vandalised and an Armed Police Battalion member was beaten. A moving bus was also attacked in Kashiani.
On November 15, BNP offices, shops and a party leader’s property were attacked in Tungipara. A Grameen Bank branch and a BNP leader’s house were also set on fire. The following day, crude bombs were allegedly hurled during a procession in Kotalipara.
Violence escalated on November 17, when four vehicles and the Tungipara Police Station office were attacked and set ablaze. Four law enforcement vehicles were also torched at Nilfa Bazar. The residence of the Gopalganj-3 lawmaker and six other houses were vandalised and set on fire.
The most widespread attacks occurred on November 19 across four upazilas.
In Muksudpur, the upazila parishad’s CCTV cameras, police station, three Grameen Bank branches and the local BNP office were vandalised or set on fire.
In Kashiani, the home of Gopalganj-1 lawmaker Md Selimuzzaman Molla and residences of BNP leaders and activists came under attack.
In Haishur village, Rajpat Union, four Hindu families involved in BNP politics were targeted. According to victims and local residents, attackers vandalised and looted eight houses, five businesses and a poultry farm. The families remain fearful, and no case has been filed.
In Kotalipara, the house and business of the municipal BNP general secretary were attacked. In Sadar, an SRB vehicle was vandalised on the Dhaka-Khulna highway, while a supermarket, restaurant and other businesses were looted.
Araf General Hospital and Diagnostic Centre, owned by the Gopalganj-2 lawmaker, and his residence were set on fire. A BNP office and another party leader’s house were also attacked.
Further incidents were reported on November 23, when more than a dozen shops at Sadar launch ghat were vandalised and looted and the sub-registry office was attacked. A Jubo Dal leader’s shop was set on fire in Kotalipara. The latest incident in the record was the vandalism of a Grameen Bank branch in Sadar’s Satpara Union on November 25.
Security forces remain deployed across the district, with 55 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh, 15 platoons of Ansar and around 2,000 police personnel.
Gopalganj Science and Technology University has been closed indefinitely, with online classes continuing since November 22. Train services in the district also remain suspended.

item.title: Edu minister finds just one student during surprise college visit in Rajshahi
item.description:
Education and Primary and Mass Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon found only one student attending class during a surprise visit to Birdalha College in Puthia upazila of Rajshahi on Thursday morning. He expressed dissatisfaction with teachers' explanations for the poor attendance.
During the visit, the minister entered a classroom and found only one female student present. He then asked a female teacher about the whereabouts of the other students.
"Where are the students? Where are my students?" he asked.
The teacher replied that only one female student was present in the classroom. Asked about the total number of students, she said the college had 15 female students.
"Don't the girls attend classes?" the minister asked.
"No, they don't. Only one has come today," the teacher replied.
Another teacher said the students had yet to enter the classroom, although the teachers had arrived on time. Asked when classes were scheduled to begin, the teacher said the class was set for 11:30 am.
The teacher further explained that students might still be outside even after teachers had entered the classroom. She also said students were reluctant to attend classes and often had to be contacted by phone to persuade them to come.
The minister expressed dissatisfaction with the teachers' explanations.
He instructed the authorities concerned to take necessary measures to improve educational standards and ensure regular attendance of both teachers and students. He also stressed the need to maintain discipline at educational institutions and ensure greater commitment to classroom teaching.
The minister was accompanied by National Parliament Whip and Advocate M. Ruhul Quddus Talukdar Dulu, Senior Secretary of the Secondary and Higher Education Division Abdul Khaleque, and Director General of the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education Professor Dr. Khan Moinuddin Al Mahmud Sohel.

item.title: Fake female doctor detained at DMCH
item.description:
