Gopalganj: Most mobile banking services suspended
item.description:
Train services to and from Gopalganj have remained suspended for nine days following sabotage by the Awami League, whose activities are banned. Now, mobile banking services have also been suspended for most customers in the district.

Since Wednesday night, local customers have been unable to make transactions through mobile financial service (MFS) providers. The suspension has left them in difficulty. Bangladesh Bank has said the services were suspended because of suspicious transactions in Gopalganj.

Financial service providers said they received instructions from the government on Wednesday night to temporarily suspend mobile banking services in Gopalganj. Officials from two service providers, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said the services were suspended after the instructions were received from the government.

Sources at the Ministry of Home Affairs said police investigations have revealed that unusually large sums of money had recently been transferred to Gopalganj from Dhaka and various other districts. For this reason, mobile banking services are being suspended temporarily in this district alone. The services will be restored once the situation returns to normal, the sources said.

Several officials at the Ministry of Home Affairs told Prothom Alo, citing intelligence agencies, that people from different districts had taken shelter in Gopalganj to avoid arrest. There was information that money had been sent to their mobile accounts.

They said money might be channelled through financial service providers in Gopalganj to organise activities in the future. The services had therefore been suspended temporarily.

On 15 November, leaders and activists of the Awami League vandalised and set fire to various structures in Gopalganj. Train services to and from the district have been suspended since two days later.

Sources at the Ministry of Railways and the Ministry of Home Affairs said the government was not considering resuming train services on this route for now because of fears of further sabotage. Steps would be taken in this regard once the situation returned to normal, they said.

The activities of Tungipara and Muksudpur police stations, which were set on fire, will also not resume soon. Sources at the Ministry of Home Affairs said local residents had requested that the two police stations reopen. However, it would take more time to resume their operations. For now, their activities are being managed from Gopalganj Sadar Police Station.

Many customers in Gopalganj unable to make mobile financial transactions

Various government allocations for Gopalganj will also remain suspended for the time being. Of the funds allocated nationwide by the Ministry of Local Government to district councils, upazila councils, municipalities and union parishads, the third instalment for Gopalganj will not be released at present, according to sources.

These institutions usually receive financial assistance in four instalments. Sources at the ministry said the release of the instalment covering January to March for Gopalganj would remain suspended.

Meanwhile, a statement issued Thursday in the name of the Gopalganj district unit of the Awami League called for all police stations and train services to be reopened. It also demanded the restoration of development allocations and the protection of citizens’ rights.

Shops crowded, customers cannot access money

Dhiman Biswas went to withdraw money from the bKash agent outlet at Hafiz Telecom in the Gopalganj launch terminal area at around 5:30 pm on Thursday. His elder sister, Sathi Biswas, had sent him Tk 2,000 through bKash.

He had left home intending to use the money for shopping. When he tried to withdraw it, he learnt that his bKash account had been temporarily suspended. He then sought help from the agent, who confirmed that the account was closed.

Tamanna Taha, who passed her Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) examination from Gopalganj Government College, has applied for admission to Rajshahi University. Although she completed the application process, she has run into difficulties because she cannot pay the fee from her Rocket account.

After visiting several shops in the Gopalganj launch terminal area Thursday, she eventually went to Hafiz Telecom. There, she spoke about her predicament.

Tamanna said Friday was the last day to apply for admission to Rajshahi University. She had therefore wanted to complete the application and pay the fee on Thursday. But she was worried about completing the process because she could not make the payment from her Rocket account.

Customers have been left in difficulty after many personal accounts with bKash, Nagad and Rocket were suddenly suspended in Gopalganj. The suspension of these mobile financial service (MFS) accounts began on Thursday.

With their accounts closed, many customers are unable to withdraw or send money or make urgent transactions. They are trying to find out why the accounts have been suspended and how long the situation will continue.

A visit to various bKash, Nagad and Rocket agent outlets in Gopalganj town Thursday afternoon found customers crowding the shops.

Gopalganj train services, police station unlikely to reopen soon; govt allocations remain suspended

Kazi Akash, a resident of Gopalganj who works at an organisation in Dhaka, found that his bKash account had suddenly been suspended Thursday afternoon. When he called the bKash helpline to find out why, he was told that his number had been suspended for the sake of an investigation.

Kazi Akash said, “I have not received money illegally from anywhere, nor have I sent money to anyone in a suspicious manner. So why was my account suspended? The helpline did not provide any further details.”

He later learnt that the bKash accounts of many of his friends in Gopalganj had also been suspended. They are worried because so many accounts have been closed at the same time. They have received no clear information about why the accounts were suspended or when they will be reactivated. As a result, they are facing difficulties making necessary transactions.

Text messages (SMS) are being sent to the mobile phone numbers registered to the suspended accounts. The messages say, “Dear Sir/Madam, your bKash account has been temporarily suspended in accordance with MFS regulations. We regret that no action can be taken in this regard at this time.”

Mohammad Hafiz Khan Molla, owner of Hafiz Telecom in the Gopalganj launch terminal area, said at least 300 to 400 customers visited his shop since Thursday morning with problems related to the suspension of their bKash, Nagad and Rocket accounts. Many of them were leaving disappointed, he added.

When asked about the matter, Bangladesh Bank spokesperson and Executive Director Arif Hossain Khan told Prothom Alo that, under the law, MFS providers could suspend the accounts of anyone involved in suspicious transactions.

Accordingly, some accounts in the Gopalganj area had recently been suspended because they had recorded an unusually high number of suspicious transactions. This was a routine procedure followed by MFS providers, he said.

Appeal not to attack power facilities

West Zone Power Distribution Company Limited (WZPDCL) has posted a message on social media urging local electricity consumers not to attack power plants in Gopalganj.

In a post on its Facebook page Thursday, the company appealed to electricity consumers from all walks of life in Gopalganj, regardless of their political affiliations, not to target power facilities, substations, vehicles used for emergency maintenance work or the personnel involved in such work for political reasons.

108 BGB platoons deployed in 8 districts, more than half in Gopalganj

It warned that damage to the electricity supply system could result in a power outage across the entire district.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, WZPDCL executive engineer for Gopalganj district Md Main Uddin said more than 100 people had entered the office premises on 19 November, although no damage had been caused that day.

He said the appeal had been made in advance to prevent any damage to power facilities in the coming days. He urged people not to attack emergency services, warning that any such attack would lead to electricity services being suspended for everyone, causing losses for all.

On 15 November, the Awami League, its affiliated organisations and the banned Chhatra League held a procession in Gopalganj, carrying locally made weapons, including oars and sticks, machetes and Chinese axes.

That day, an armoured personnel carrier (APC) belonging to the police was set on fire and a police box was vandalised. Leaders and activists of the party also vandalised the July memorial and the nameplate at Hadi Chattar. They then set fire to the homes of three Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) lawmakers.

On 17 November, Tungipara Police Station in Gopalganj was set on fire, followed by Muksudpur Police Station on 19 November. Operations at both police stations have remained suspended since then.

Speaking about how the government was dealing with the recent activities of the Awami League, and managing the law and order situation, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told a press conference Thursday after a joint meeting at the BNP's central office in Naya Paltan that law enforcement agencies would not use excessive force.

However, if necessary to protect people's lives and property, strict measures would be taken in accordance with the law. The government has already announced this position, he said, adding that the government was committed to acting democratically.

Proposal to run trains via alternative route

Bangladesh Railway has temporarily suspended the Jahanabad Express on the Dhaka–Khulna route and the Ruposhi Bangla Express on the Dhaka–Benapole route from 19 November, citing passenger safety and the overall situation.

This has increased inconvenience for passengers and disrupted regular ticket sales. A proposal has been made to operate an alternative pair of trains on the Khulna–Poradaha–Rajbari–Dhaka route instead.

The proposal was sent to the director general of Bangladesh Railway on Wednesday by the office of the chief operating superintendent of the railway’s west zone.

Activities-banned Awami League holds protest march in Gopalganj with machetes, hockey sticks

It says a new pair of trains could be operated on the Khulna–Poradaha–Rajbari–Dhaka route from 28 November, using the carriages of the Jahanabad Express and Ruposhi Bangla Express. If the proposal is implemented, the trains will not pass through Kashiani and Muksudpur stations in Gopalganj.

The letter says the Jahanabad Express, which operates between Khulna and Dhaka, and the Ruposhi Bangla Express, which runs between Dhaka and Benapole, have had to be cancelled every day since 19 November. Repeated cancellations mean passengers have to be refunded for their tickets, creating further complications and financial losses.

Passengers are also facing inconvenience. The alternative service has been proposed to maintain rail connectivity between Khulna and Dhaka, make effective use of the train carriages and reduce financial losses.

According to the proposed timetable, the train would leave Khulna at 8:00 am and arrive in Dhaka at 3:10 pm. The return service would depart Dhaka at 4:10 pm and reach Khulna at 11:35 pm. The train would operate six days a week, with Monday as its weekly day off.

On this alternative route, it would stop at Daulatpur, Noapara, Jashore, Mobarakganj, Kotchandpur, Darshana Halt, Chuadanga, Alamdanga, Poradaha, Kushtia Court, Kumarkhali, Pangsha, Rajbari, Faridpur and Bhanga stations.

[Gopalganj Correspondent contributed information]

item.title: The hunt for a fair garment wage does not stop at Tk 17,000
item.description:
BANGLADESH-GARMENTS/

"I pity the man who wants a coat so cheap that the man or woman who produces the cloth or shapes it into a garment will starve in the process." Benjamin Harrison said these words in 1888, and the recent scenario of Bangladesh shows how true they still are.

On 25 November 2026, after a meeting that ran from the afternoon until two in the morning, the Minimum Wage Board sets the minimum wage for entry-level (grade four) garment workers at Tk 17,000, up from Tk 12,500. Workers in grades one to three will get between Tk 19,200 and Tk 21,500. The workers' representative had proposed Tk 18,000, but four of the six board members voted for Tk 17,000. The number is now fixed, but the problem is not resolved.

On the same day, 140 factories in Gazipur, Savar and Ashulia remained closed as workers blocked highways, saying the raise is still not enough to support their families. The question is no longer only how large the raise should be, but what a 36 per cent increase will do to workers, to factories and to the wider economy?

The reason behind this demand has not changed. High inflation has sharply increased the cost of food, housing, transport, healthcare and other daily necessities. Point to point inflation stood at 8.27 per cent in October 2026, according to Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) data show that inflation has outpaced wage growth for 57 consecutive months. Workers' representatives had earlier demanded Tk 32,000.

The Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) estimated that a family of four needs Tk 18,578 to stay above the upper poverty line and Tk 24,204 for a living wage. BGMEA questioned CPD's assumptions about household size and earning members, and CPD itself cautioned that its figures were illustrative, since there is no large, representative survey of RMG workers. Even so, it is worth noticing that the final wage of Tk 17,000 sits below even the lower end of CPD's range.

Wage board vote fixes minimum wage at Tk 17,000

For workers, the first question is how much of this 36 per cent is a real gain. A raise in Taka is not the same as a raise in what Taka can buy. The Tk 12,500 wage was set in December 2023, and prices have kept rising for almost three years since then, hence a large portion of the new increase only makes up for ground that was already lost. Workers with longer service have recovered some of it through the yearly increment, which the government raised from 5 per cent to 9 per cent in December 2024, but new entrants have not. If inflation stays near 8 per cent, the real value of Tk 17,000 will also shrink every month until the next review.

The risk is that a higher minimum wage creates fewer but better paid formal jobs, while those who lose them move to informal work with no wage protection at all. At the same time, a rise in RMG wages could pull workers away from other sectors, creating labour shortages elsewhere and making those industries less efficient.

There is also the question of who finally keeps the raise. A study by Awaj Foundation on the 2023 wage increase, covering 60 factories, found that most workers did receive the revised wage, but rising rent, transport, education and healthcare costs reduced their purchasing power, and many still depended on loans to meet basic needs.

In industrial areas, most workers rent rooms near the factory and buy from the same local shops. When their income rises and there is no change in the supply of housing, a part of the raise can pass to landlords through higher rent. A wage increase on paper may therefore become a smaller increase in the worker's actual living standard.

Unemployment is another vital concern, as the higher cost burden may push businesses to lay off workers and cut production. The same Awaj study found that around one third of workers reported layoffs after the last wage increase, along with higher production targets and more pressure at the workplace. In other words, factories adjust not only by cutting jobs but also by asking fewer workers to produce more.

At a Daily Star discussion on 15 November 2026, Fazlee Shamim Ehsan of the Bangladesh Employers' Federation said the number of helpers on one production line in his factory had fallen from about 26 to just 3, and that many workers are now looking for informal jobs, such as driving electric rickshaws. The risk is that a higher minimum wage creates fewer but better paid formal jobs, while those who lose them move to informal work with no wage protection at all. At the same time, a rise in RMG wages could pull workers away from other sectors, creating labour shortages elsewhere and making those industries less efficient.

For the industry, BGMEA says production costs have already risen by 25 to 30 per cent over the last three years, and 287 factories have closed during that period. At a dialogue organised by Voice for Reform on 25 November 2026, BGMEA vice-president Md Shehab Udduza Chowdhury said that a minimum wage of Tk 17,000 actually costs a factory about Tk 25,000 per worker each month after accounting bonuses and overtime. Former BGMEA president Rubana Huq warned that many small and medium factories could shut down in the coming months. The burden will not fall equally. Large factories with modern machines, direct buyers and access to credit can absorb some of the cost by raising productivity. Small subcontracting factories, which already work on thin margins, cannot do this easily. The raise may therefore speed up a shift towards fewer and bigger factories. That may improve average productivity over time, but sudden closures without an orderly exit system leave workers without jobs and owed wages.

The financial sector would be affected as well. Even before this wage increase, around one third of all bank loans in Bangladesh were non-performing, based on Bangladesh Bank data. If higher costs squeeze factories' profit margins, more of them may struggle to repay their loans, raising default risk for banks. Factories would also find it harder to expand, which would hurt not only employment but also economic growth and living standards.

The wider economy will feel the effect through prices too. A higher wage raises the cost of production, and when workers' spending power rises at the same time, cost-push and demand-pull pressures can work together in the short run. The cost-push effect may be smaller than it first appears, since most garments are sold abroad rather than in local markets. The demand-pull effect is more real. Garment workers spend almost all of their income on food, rent and transport, so nearly every extra Taka goes straight into local markets. The pressure on national inflation is likely to be modest, but prices in industrial areas could rise faster, which takes us back to the problem of the raise being eaten away before it reaches the worker's plate.

How much have garment workers’ wages increased in each grade?

The damage could also go beyond the domestic level. Bangladesh's biggest advantage in the world market is low cost. According to H&M Group data reported by Prothom Alo, Bangladesh's minimum wage of USD 102 was lower than India's USD 124, Vietnam's USD 163 and Cambodia's USD 208. At the Bangladesh Bank rate of about Tk 124 per dollar in early November 2026, Tk 17,000 is roughly USD 137. This would place Bangladesh above India, but still below Vietnam and Cambodia. That is a much smaller risk than the Tk 32,000 demand, which would have put Bangladesh above all three. Still, some buyers of basic, low-margin items may shift orders to India, which would put more pressure on Bangladesh's trade balance, which is already in deficit.

Wages should be based on real statistics about what workers spend and what factories can pay, and reviewed every year against inflation, so that anger does not build up for three years at a time. The government should also reduce the costs that have nothing to do with wages, such as gas and electricity shortages, extortion and bureaucratic delays, instead of letting factories pass them on to workers. International buyers, who gain the most from cheap Bangladeshi garments, should also carry part of the cost through fair prices.

The deeper concern is not only the wage but the price that Bangladesh receives for its garments. At the same Voice for Reform dialogue, RAPID chairman Mohammad Abdur Razzaque said Bangladesh receives the lowest unit prices among competing countries, so buyers capture much of the gain from workers' productivity. If buyers paid even slightly more per unit, much of the new wage could be absorbed. But Rubana Huq warned that buyers rarely pay more just because costs have risen, and may ask for price cuts in later seasons.

Voice for Reform proposed a gradual adjustment of the exchange rate to raise exporters' Taka earnings. However, a weaker Taka also makes imported food and fuel more expensive, which pushes up the same living costs that the wage increase was meant to cover. The tool that helps factories can quietly cut into the worker's real wage.

Neither side is wrong to be tensed. Workers find it difficult to live properly even on Tk 17,000 after nearly five years of prices rising faster than wages. Factory owners, meanwhile, say they can barely absorb this increase, while orders are uncertain and banks are already weighed down by bad loans. The answer will not come from a number won on the highway or held back in a boardroom, and this round has shown that clearly, as roads were blocked even after the board had voted.

The real reform needed is in the process. CPD's Towfiqul Islam Khan has argued that wage setting should be based on scientific evidence, not bargaining, with the wage board formed six months before each review and a permanent wage commission supported by BBS. Wages should be based on real statistics about what workers spend and what factories can pay, and reviewed every year against inflation, so that anger does not build up for three years at a time.

The government should also reduce the costs that have nothing to do with wages, such as gas and electricity shortages, extortion and bureaucratic delays, instead of letting factories pass them on to workers. International buyers, who gain the most from cheap Bangladeshi garments, should also carry part of the cost through fair prices.

To conclude, Benjamin Harrison pitied the person who wants a coat so cheap that its maker starves. Bangladesh should remember the other half of that lesson too, as a coat priced so high that no one buys it leaves the same worker without a job. At Tk 17,000, Bangladesh now stands between these two dangers. Whether this becomes a fair wage that depend less on the number itself and more on what is done after it.


Md Sadi Jashim is a student at BRAC University. He can be reached at samsadsadi388@gmail.com.

Rajshahi’s Mission Hospital: Evergreen even after crossing a century
item.description:
The Christian Mission Hospital in Rajshahi city has passed the century mark. It is now busier than ever. Shishir Moral writes about the hospital.

Early last year, Ahmed Ehsanur Rahman—a scientist at the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b) and a member of the Health Sector Reform Commission formed during the interim government—told me the story of an old hospital record-keeping system. It was the story of the Christian Mission Hospital in Rajshahi city. For decades, the hospital had meticulously recorded the birth details of every child delivered there; such a “Birth Register” is rarely seen.

Since the late 1980s, I had visited Rajshahi city many times, yet I had never been to the Christian Mission Hospital. Hearing about the Birth Register from Ehsanur sparked my desire to see the facility. In April 2025, Ehsanur and I spent half a day touring the hospital.

Subsequently, at the beginning of December last year, I visited the hospital again and stayed at its guesthouse for two days. Walking through hospitals is a habit of mine, and this visit was no exception—I made methodical rounds morning, afternoon, and night, speaking with patients, guards, officials, nurses, physicians, and administrators. My greatest curiosity centred on the Birth Register.

Later, on 18 December last year, my report on the hospital was published in Prothom Alo. The hospital has now crossed the 100-year milestone. Due to the country’s political situation last year, the hospital authorities did not feel comfortable organising any centenary celebrations; those events are taking place on 26 and 27 November.

A 100-year journey

Across various countries and regions of Asia and Africa, the arrival of Christianity was often accompanied by education and healthcare, giving rise to schools and hospitals. Christian Mission Hospital shares a similar history, chronicled in a souvenir published to mark its centenary. Although formally established in 1926, its seeds were sown several decades earlier.

Following the Great Rebellion of 1857–58, the Presbyterian Church of England decided to open a mission in Rajshahi. At their request, Bengali evangelist Reverend Behari Lal Singh from Kolkata arrived in Rampur Boalia in 1862, beginning his work by setting up a village primary school and a prayer hall. After his death in 1874, his widow single-handedly carried on the mission of educating women and girls for three years.

►This history is recounted in a commemorative publication prepared to mark the institution’s centenary. Although the hospital was established in 1926, its roots go back several decades further. ►The central vision of the hospital’s future plans is to combine modern medical science and higher education while preserving its heritage and commitment to compassionate care, so that people in northern Bangladesh can access world-class healthcare at affordable prices.

In late 1877, a young Scottish physician, Donald Morison, arrived in Rajshahi and began treating patients. He trained local youths as “dressers” and went on to establish a small five-bed hospital in 1887, launching regular medical services in 1890.

Later, JA McDonald Smith arrived in Rajshahi in 1900, followed by Donald Morison’s son, Robert Morison, in 1904. In 1911, Smith built the first full-fledged hospital on the banks of the Tulshiganga River, midway between Naogaon and Santahar. However, due to crises stemming from the First World War and acute shortages in human resources, the Naogaon hospital closed in 1923, though its building still stands today.

In a vaulted room of the main building, the hospital’s founding history is inscribed on white stone: construction began on 22 October 1924 and was completed in January 1926. The builder was Babu CK Das, and the chief mason was Azmat Mistri.

The hospital embarked on its permanent journey in 1926 when Robert Morison and Bengali Hindu physician Bhupendranath Bhaya jointly launched permanent operations at the Boalia Mission Compound. That same year, the “Westminster Hostel” was constructed in Srirampur to house Hindu and Muslim students of Rajshahi College. The hostel building later became the hospital’s permanent address.

When Robert Morison departed in 1929, Bhupendranath Bhaya single-handedly kept the hospital alive until 1940 by running the outpatient department. In 1932, Reverend Priya Kumar Baroi joined as pastor, remaining associated with the institution for half a century. During the Second World War and the Bengal Famine of 1943, Himangshu Kumar Sarkar and Haripada Guha took the helm. Following the Partition of India in 1947, Westminster Hostel fell vacant after Hindu students migrated to India.

In 1948, Scottish surgeon Ian Patrick and Bengali physician Upendranath Malakar assumed responsibility. Aided by more than 20 beds donated free of charge from the Ranaghat Mission Hospital in India—which had closed after Partition—and four male nurses who came from there (Kshitish Chandra Baroi, Francis Hiranmoy Bepari, Harendranath Sarkar, and Indubhushan Mondal), the hospital was reborn in April 1950 inside the converted Westminster Hostel. In 1953, Scottish physician Elizabeth Conan joined the hospital, serving for 21 years.

Liberation War and beyond

During the Liberation War of 1971, the hospital closed temporarily when roughly 120 staff members—including physicians Malakar and Conan, and sister Jean Degenhardt—took refuge in India, though the building remained intact. Following independence, the “Elizabeth Conan Memorial Nursing Institute” was established in 1973, and a children’s ward opened in 1974 with support from the city of Kristiansand in Norway. When the Church of Bangladesh was formed in 1974, the hospital came under its administration.

After physician Malakar retired, the proliferation of new private clinics across the city subjected the hospital to stiff competition and financial strain, yet it never shut down completely. It launched a Community Health Programme in 1989, an Eye Clinic in 1991, and a Primary Healthcare Programme in 1994—supported by American missionary physicians Leslie and Cynthia Morgan—extending medical services to 29 villages.

During the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, the hospital contracted with the government to treat coronavirus patients for six months. Afterwards, fears of infection and a dilapidated physical structure left it devoid of patients and on the brink of closure. Under the leadership of Church of Bangladesh Moderator Bishop Samuel Sunil Mankhin and the Board of Trustees, Pradip Chand Mondal took over as Chief Executive Officer in January 2021. He renovated the buildings, introduced modern medical equipment, and overhauled the administrative structure. With specialist physicians joining from 2022 onward, the hospital rebounded in full swing. The institution is celebrating its centenary under the slogan “The Hospital That Stayed.”

Official records

The Rajshahi District Gazetteer, published in 1976, records another account of the hospital’s history. According to the gazetteer, Christian Mission Hospital began its work in Rajshahi city in 1877, commencing regular hospital operations in 1890, though activities slowed between 1937 and 1948 due to staffing shortages. Constructed at its current site in 1950, the 66-bed facility housed children’s, women’s, and men’s wards, drawing patients from Khulna, Jashore, Kushtia, Pabna, Bogura, Dinajpur, and Rangpur.

The gazetteer also provides patient statistics for 1966: 1,426 inpatients were admitted for treatment that year (an average of five admissions daily), while 14,005 patients received outpatient care (averaging 45 outpatients a day).

The old publication further reveals financial figures: in the 1965–66 fiscal year, the hospital earned Tk 157,612.38, alongside Tk 38,043.82 in grants from England, against total expenditure of Tk 192,303.79.

A modern information system in the past

Christian Mission Hospital preserves patient records with remarkable care. Precisely how far back this practice of recording birth details goes is unknown, though a 66-year-old “Birth Register” still survives. Hospital CEO Pradip Chand Mondal told Prothom Alo, “Alongside renovations for the hospital’s centenary, we began organising the library and uncovered these old ledgers—as well as books and documents even older than the registers. These are priceless assets.” Indeed, they are priceless assets for the entire country.

The Birth Register logs the date of each delivery, the names and addresses of the mother and her husband, foetal position, mode of delivery (normal or Caesarean), the baby’s sex and birth weight, and the names of the attending chief physician, midwife, and assisting nurses, accompanied by a brief clinical note on the physical condition of both mother and newborn—all written neatly in fountain pen.

The oldest ledger recovered by hospital authorities contains an entry in English reading: “Mrs. Makbul, admitted 13 December 1959 at 6:15 pm. Membranes ruptured at 1:15 am. Normal delivery completed at 1:28 am. Placenta and membranes expelled completely at 1:35 am. Minimal bleeding. The condition of mother and newborn is good.”

The ledger further notes that this was Mrs Makbul’s second child—a live female infant who cried vigorously at birth and weighed 4 pounds 7 ounces. It stands as a testament to sound healthcare practice, and such records are invaluable treasures for public health researchers.

The hospital today

At the turn of its century, the hospital is busier than at any point in its history. Today, it operates 135 beds with nearly 100 specialist physicians serving regularly across various departments. On average, around 7,650 patients receive outpatient treatment every month (an average of 228 patients daily in 2026), with women and children accounting for roughly 60 per cent of all patients.

About 1,500 inpatients are admitted monthly, and more than 100 patients receive inpatient care in the wards on any given day. The hospital places special emphasis on normal deliveries: whereas 7 per cent of births were normal deliveries in 2021, that figure has more than quadrupled to 30 per cent in 2026.

New dreams

The core philosophy of the hospital’s future blueprint is to blend modern medical science and higher education—through medical and nursing colleges—while preserving its heritage and compassionate care, ensuring people in northern Bangladesh have access to affordable, world-class treatment and creating employment for future generations. 

CEO Pradip Chand Mondal has unveiled a vision to establish three major educational and service institutions in the coming years: a Medical College, a Nursing College, and an Institute of Health Technology—alongside achieving financial self-reliance, maintaining care for the underprivileged, and expanding primary healthcare services.

* Shishir Morol is a Special Correspondent at Prothom Alo. The opinions expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Artistic craftsmanship on the sea sand
item.description:
Alongside the beauty of ocean waves, sandy beaches, and jhau (casuarina) groves, artistic diversity has now been added to the mix. Spread across roughly 35 acres of the casuarina forest along Cox’s Bazar beach, the three-month-long "Cox’s Bazar Tourism Beach Carnival" has kicked off.

Organised by the Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation, the round-the-clock festival began on 22 November and will continue until 31 January. Sand sculptures of tigers, elephants, the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban (National Parliament Building), the Shaheed Minar, and various other artworks have been crafted for the festival.

Artists from the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Canada are also participating in creating these sculptures. A replica of a whale has been fashioned out of reusable plastic items, while the vulnerable lives of working people impacted by climate change are also portrayed in the artists' creations. Tourists are flocking to see these artworks.

item.title: Stolen childhoods: Why Bangladesh must scrap section 19 of the Child Marriage Act
item.description:
Imagine the combined population of the ASEAN nations, or that of Latin America and the Caribbean. Nearly as many women and girls alive in 2026 were married as children worldwide -- an estimated 650 million, including 44 million in Bangladesh.
Today, the world observes the inaugural International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage, following a United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) resolution adopted in September proclaiming November 27 as the day to galvanize global efforts against this crisis. While the observance offers a vital opportunity for collective action, Bangladesh faces a sobering reality: It has one of the highest rates of child marriage in the world.
According to the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, the proportion of women aged 20--24 who were married before the age of 18 declined from 51.4% in 2019 to 47.2%, marking slow and modest progress. However, the survey reveals an alarming reversal among younger adolescents: 38.9% of girls aged 15--19 are currently married, up from 32.9% in 2019. This six-percentage-point increase erases 13 years of hard-won progress, taking the country back to the 39% rate recorded in 2006. Globally, around 12 million girls are married before turning 18 every year.
South Asia bears the heaviest burden, with roughly 285 million women and girls who were married as children -- about 45% of the global total. While India has the highest absolute number because of its population size, Bangladesh ranks among the countries with the highest prevalence of child marriage.
As we mark this UN-designated day, we must confront the harsh realities robbing Bangladeshi girls of their childhoods. Too many adolescents remain trapped in a vicious cycle in which early marriage leads to premature pregnancies, jeopardizing maternal and neonatal health, and contributing to child malnutrition -- threatening the very future of our nation.
A major driver of this crisis is a regressive legal loophole introduced in 2017. While countries generally replace archaic laws with more progressive and modern legislation, Bangladesh took a step backwards when it passed the Child Marriage Restraint Act (CMRA) 2017, replacing the colonial-era 1929 law but undermining the universal minimum marriage age of 18. Section 19 of the 2017 Act allows child marriage below the age of 18 under undefined "special circumstances" and with court approval.
From the outset, rights advocates and the media warned that the provision could undermine the law. At the time, the government dismissed these concerns, assuring stakeholders that the enforcement rules to be introduced later would impose strict restrictions on the provision. However, when the CMRA Rules were issued in 2018, they failed to introduce meaningful safeguards.
The MICS 2025 findings now lay bare the cost of this failure. In a country proud of its economic and infrastructural progress, nearly two in five girls aged 15-19 are married. This regression comes even as global child marriage prevalence has declined by 15% over the past decade, from one in four girls (25%) to roughly one in five (21%), representing 25 million fewer child marriages.
Along with India, Pakistan, and parts of sub-Saharan Africa, Bangladesh continues to bear a disproportionate share of the global burden. Meanwhile, in Latin America and the Caribbean, where informal unions are common, progress has stagnated for 25 years, putting the region on track to surpass South Asia in child marriage prevalence by 2030.
Child marriage has devastating consequences. It cuts short girls' education, limits their economic independence, threatens their physical and mental health, and exposes them to domestic and sexual violence, depriving them of their fundamental freedoms.
To be fair, the CMRA 2017 and its 2018 Rules have provided a foundational framework for interventions, including during the Covid-19 pandemic. Public awareness and law enforcement efforts have improved, while communities increasingly use national helplines, including 109, 1098, and 999 to report and prevent impending child marriages.
However, these positive efforts have been undermined by several fundamental flaws in the legislation:
Rather than closing the loophole, the 2018 Rules have widened it, leaving minors vulnerable to forced and premature marriages.
It is better late than never. Bangladesh must urgently review and amend Section 19 of the CMRA 2017 and overhaul the ambiguous 2018 Rules. A country approaching graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category cannot afford to lose its future workforce and leadership to a cycle of early marriage, unplanned pregnancies, and childhood malnutrition.
The UNGA resolution adopted last September calls on member states to implement comprehensive, multisectoral national strategies, invest in quality education -- including opportunities for married girls to return to school -- and empower women and girls.
If Bangladesh is serious about honouring the spirit of this inaugural International Day, it must begin by fixing its laws and guaranteeing adolescent girls the childhood, health, and future they deserve.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Pubali Bank achieves international recognition for excellence in Islamic banking
item.description:
Pubali Bank PLC has achieved yet another milestone in its banking journey by winning the “Best Islamic Banking Window in Bangladesh – 2026” award at the 12th Islamic Retail Banking Awards (IRBA), organized by UK-based Cambridge IFA.
The award was recently received on behalf of the bank by Mohammad Humayun Kabir, general manager & head of Islamic banking wing, from Mohamed Waheed Hassan, former president of the Maldives, at a ceremony held in Karachi, Pakistan, in the presence of Prof Humayon Dar, chairman of Cambridge IFA.
To celebrate this achievement, chairman Monzurur Rahman, along with directors Habibur Rahman, Rumana Sharif, Azizur Rahman, Md Abdur Razzak Mondal, Rana Laila Hafiz, Arif Ahmed Choudhury, Shahinuzzaman Yaqub and Sajid Azad; independent directors Mohammad Naushad Ali Chowdhury and Hasina Sheykh; managing director Mohammad Ali; and deputy managing director Mohammad Shahadat Hossain, cut a cake in a festive atmosphere.
Members of the Shariah supervisory committee Mufti Muhammad Abu Sayeed Khan and Hafiz Prof Mohammad Nurullah, CSAA; general manager & company secretary Md Anisur Rahman; general manager & chief financial officer Mohammad Liton Miah, general manager & head of Islamic banking wing Mohammad Humayun Kabir; general manager & chief protocol officer Md. Shah Alam; and other senior executives of the bank joined the celebration.
This international recognition reflects Pubali Bank’s unwavering commitment to Shariah-compliant banking, service excellence and customer trust.

item.title: Al-Arafah Islami Bank holds agent banking meeting, courtyard gathering in Sirajganj
item.description:
To bring modern Shariah-based banking services to underserved communities, expand agent banking operations, and improve customer service, Al-Arafah Islami Bank PLC organized a discussion meeting and courtyard gathering in Shahjadpur, Sirajganj.
The event was held on November 26, Thursday, at the seminar room of PPD Trust, Shahjadpur.
Owners of 14 agent banking outlets under Shahjadpur Branch, bank officials working at the outlets, and officials and employees of the branch attended the program.
The program was attended by Md Aminul Islam Bhuiyan, deputy managing director of the bank, as chief guest.
Md Mainul Islam, senior vice president and head of agent banking, attended as special guest.
The session was presided over by Md Mesbahul Monir, manager of Shahjadpur Branch.
Md Aminul Islam Bhuiyan said that agent banking is helping bring modern Shariah-based banking services to people in remote areas. To further accelerate this initiative, he emphasized acquiring new customers, bringing expatriate income into formal banking channels, engaging more people in Mudaraba savings schemes and maintaining regular communication with customers.
He also urged outlet operators to provide timely services, ensure proper KYC compliance and safeguard the confidentiality of customer information to establish each outlet as a trusted banking destination.
Md Mainul Islam advised the outlet operators to maintain scheduled operating hours, ensure adequate cash availability and uninterrupted network connectivity, and familiarize customers with the bank’s various digital services.
The meeting reviewed the performance of the agent banking outlets and identified measures to expand business and improve customer service during the remaining period of the year.
During the open discussion, agents and outlet officials shared their field-level experiences, opportunities and challenges.
The programme also announced a decision to select the best outlet every month to recognize and encourage outstanding performance.
Al-Arafah Islami Bank PLC continues to work towards bringing Shariah-compliant banking services to urban and remote communities across the country through its branches, sub-branches and agent banking outlets.

item.title: National Film Award winner Matia Banu Shuku passes away
item.description:
National Film Award-winning producer, director and screenwriter Matia Banu Shuku has passed away.
She breathed her last at around 12:05am on Friday after being transferred from the intensive care unit (ICU) to palliative care late Thursday night.
Cultural activist Ershadul Haque Tinku confirmed her death.
According to family sources, her body will be taken to Bakultala on the premises of Dhaka University's Faculty of Fine Arts at 5am, following Fajr prayers.
She will lie in state there until 10:30am to allow people to pay their last respects.
At 11am, her body will be taken to the Central Shaheed Minar for public tributes before being taken to Dhaka University Central Mosque, where her first namaz-e-janaza will be held after Jumma prayers.
She will then be taken to the Uttara Sector 12 Graveyard for burial.
Matia Banu Shuku, the eldest daughter of Language Movement veteran Abdul Matin and wife of filmmaker Nurul Alam Atique, had been suffering from cancer and kidney complications for a long time.

item.title: SRB nabs Shibganj blast suspect from Rajshahi hideout
item.description:
A man injured in a crude bomb explosion while allegedly making explosives in Chapainawabganj’s Shibganj has been arrested in Rajshahi.
The arrestee, Nazmul Karim, also known as Nurul, was secretly receiving treatment at a house in Rajshahi city after fleeing the scene of the explosion.
Members of the Special Response Battalion (SRB-5) detained him during a raid on a house in the city’s Tero Khadia Paschimpara area around 8:30pm on Thursday. He was later taken to Rajshahi Medical College Hospital (RMCH) for treatment.
Nazmul hails from Parchouka village in Shibganj upazila. He runs a tea stall in the area and is locally known as a crude bomb maker. SRB-5 claimed that he is an activist of the activities-banned Awami League.
At the time of the raid, Nazmul was receiving an intravenous saline infusion. SRB personnel took him to the hospital in their ambulance, along with his wife and a female tenant of the house.
According to police and local sources, an explosion occurred around noon on Wednesday while cocktails were being made in Parchouka village. Thomas Ali was killed on the spot.
Thomas was the personal assistant to former Awami League lawmaker Dr Samil Uddin Ahmed Shimul, who represented the Chapainawabganj-1 (Shibganj) constituency.
He was the son of Md Mortuza of Bishwanathpur Lambar Tola village in the upazila. On his Facebook profile, Thomas identified himself as a member of the Shibganj upazila unit of the Krishak League and an Awami League activist. His profile also featured photographs of him attending various Awami League programmes.
Three others injured in the explosion fled the scene, including Nazmul. He initially received treatment at a private clinic in Rajshahi before taking shelter at a rented house in Tero Khadia Paschimpara belonging to a woman known to him.
The house is owned by Md Alauddin, a retired professor of the English Department at Rajshahi College.
A female tenant of the house, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Nazmul was previously known to them. His wife brought him to the house on Wednesday after he received treatment at the clinic.
They had planned to return to their village home on Thursday after having his wounds dressed, she said. However, an unidentified man arrived around noon and administered saline to Nazmul. SRB personnel surrounded the house later that evening.
The woman said she did not know how Nazmul had been injured. However, during his stay, he told her that he had been at the scene of the explosion and had been taken there on a motorcycle.
SRB-5 Commanding Officer Lieutenant Colonel Md Foysal Istiaq said Nazmul was the only person detained from the house.
He said Nazmul was taken to RMCH as he required medical attention and would remain under police custody while receiving treatment.
He added that Nazmul would be shown arrested in the case filed over the explosion and produced before a court after recovering.

item.title: BADC chairman stresses transparency, accountability in implementing development plans
item.description:
Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) held a farewell program for its Chairman Md Azizul Islam at the conference room of the corporation’s headquarters at Krishi Bhaban on Thursday following his transfer.
Heads of all wings and divisions, representatives of professional organizations, and officials from different levels attended the program, said a press release.
Speaking at the event, Azizul Islam said BADC was one of the country's oldest and most traditional institutions, with a vital role in agriculture and agricultural production.
He said the corporation had earned farmers' trust by ensuring the effective delivery of essential agricultural inputs and services, including quality seeds, non-urea fertilizers, and irrigation facilities, to farmers' doorsteps.
He also noted that the scope of the corporation's activities had been expanding over the years. Implementing annual work plans with less than half of its approved workforce was both a major challenge and a significant achievement, he added.
Highlighting key initiatives, he stressed the need to ensure the timely supply of fertilizers, excavate and re-excavate canals, and implement measures to achieve self-sufficiency in onion and jute seed production for the first time.

item.title: Gopalganj may face power cuts if political attacks target facilities
item.description:
The Gopalganj Electricity Supply Division of the West Zone Power Distribution Company Ltd (WZPDCL) has urged political activists to refrain from attacking power installations, substations, maintenance vehicles and personnel amid political programmes and violence.
The division has warned that any politically motivated damage to power infrastructure could disrupt electricity supply across the district.
The warning was issued in a press release by the WZPDCL's Gopalganj Electricity Supply Division on Thursday morning.
The press release urged all concerned to refrain from targeting power installations, substations, vehicles and personnel engaged in emergency maintenance work for political reasons. It warned that any damage to the power distribution system could lead to a complete suspension of electricity supply across Gopalganj.
Confirming the matter, WZPDCL Gopalganj Executive Engineer Md Main Uddin said around 100 to 150 people attacked the electricity office during a lockdown on November 19.
"Several glass panels at the office were vandalised. The attackers also threatened staff, saying that a portrait of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman that had been put up must not be removed. The incident left employees terrified," he said.
He said further political programmes and another lockdown were expected, warning that attacks on power installations, substations or electricity lines, as well as vandalism and cable-cutting, could disrupt electricity supply.
"Amid such security concerns, employees may be afraid to go out for emergency repairs. In that situation, we may have no alternative but to suspend electricity supply," he added.
The executive engineer said people from all political parties and walks of life in Gopalganj are consumers of the electricity department, and ensuring uninterrupted power supply to everyone, regardless of political affiliation, is its responsibility.
"Any damage to power infrastructure caused by a political group would leave people across the district suffering. Considering this, we posted the appeal on Facebook to alert consumers and raise public awareness," he said.

item.title: Milon calls for steps to boost classroom attendance
item.description:
Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Haque Milon has expressed dissatisfaction over poor student attendance during a surprise visit to Biraldah College in Puthia upazila of Rajshahi on Thursday.
He directed the authorities concerned to take necessary steps to improve the quality of education and ensure the regular attendance of both teachers and students.
During the November 26 visit, the minister inspected several classrooms and found only one female student present in one of them. He questioned the teachers about the low attendance but was not satisfied with their explanations.
The teachers informed him that the college had 15 female students, but only one was present that day. They also acknowledged that students were generally reluctant to attend classes regularly.
The minister subsequently instructed the authorities to take appropriate measures to improve educational standards and ensure regular attendance in classrooms.
After the inspection, he urged students to maintain discipline in their academic activities and pay greater attention to their studies.
National Parliament Whip Advocate M Ruhul Quddus Talukdar Dulu, Secondary and Higher Education Division Senior Secretary Abdul Khaleque, and Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education Director General Professor Dr Khan Moineuddin Al Mahmud Sohel were also present during the visit.
